Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "Pointwise values of the CDF … correspond to expected values of an indicator function, $C(x)\equiv\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{P<x}]\equiv\mathbb E[H(x-P)]$, where $H(x)$ is the Heaviside step function. To improve the multilevel variance, this is smoothed to give $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $x<-1$, and $g(x)=1$ for $x>1$. The parameter $\delta$ controls the degree of smoothing. As $\delta\to0$, $g(x/\delta)\to H(x)$, and the accuracy improves but the variance of the multilevel estimator increases." 

Let $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $g(y)=0$ for $y<-1$ and $g(y)=1$ for $y>1$, and let $y\ne0$. Then for all sufficiently small $\delta>0$, $g(y/\delta)=H(y)$, where $H(y)=1$ if $y>0$ and $0$ otherwise.
MLMC.smooth_step_eventually.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.7, p. 46.

MLMC.abs_smoothCDF_sub_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.7: the smoothed CDF $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$ differs from $C(x)=\mathbb P(P<x)$ by at most $\mathbb P(|P-x|\le\delta)$
MLMC.abs_smoothCDF_sub_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "Pointwise values of the CDF … correspond to expected values of an indicator function, $C(x)\equiv\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{P<x}]\equiv\mathbb E[H(x-P)]$, where $H(x)$ is the Heaviside step function. To improve the multilevel variance, this is smoothed to give $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $x<-1$, and $g(x)=1$ for $x>1$. The parameter $\delta$ controls the degree of smoothing. As $\delta\to0$, $g(x/\delta)\to H(x)$, and the accuracy improves but the variance of the multilevel estimator increases." 

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $P:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ measurable, and $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ measurable with $0\le g\le1$, $g(y)=0$ for $y<-1$ and $g(y)=1$ for $y>1$. Then for all $\delta>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$
\big|\mathrm{smoothCDF}(\mathbb P,P,g,\delta,x)-\mathbb P(P<x)\big|\le\mathbb P(|P-x|\le\delta).
$$
MLMC.abs_smoothCDF_sub_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.7, p. 46.
MLMC.abs_smoothCDF_sub_le.explanation: Pointwise, $g((x-P)/\delta)=\mathbf 1_{P<x}$ where $|P-x|>\delta$, and the two differ by at most $1$ elsewhere.

MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.7: as $\delta\to0^+$ the smoothed CDF converges to the CDF, $C_\delta(x)\to\mathbb P(P<x)$, when $P$ has no atom at $x$
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "Pointwise values of the CDF … correspond to expected values of an indicator function, $C(x)\equiv\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{P<x}]\equiv\mathbb E[H(x-P)]$, where $H(x)$ is the Heaviside step function. To improve the multilevel variance, this is smoothed to give $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $x<-1$, and $g(x)=1$ for $x>1$. The parameter $\delta$ controls the degree of smoothing. As $\delta\to0$, $g(x/\delta)\to H(x)$, and the accuracy improves but the variance of the multilevel estimator increases." 

With the hypotheses of `abs_smoothCDF_sub_le`, let $x\in\mathbb R$ with $\mathbb P(P=x)=0$. Then $\mathrm{smoothCDF}(\mathbb P,P,g,\delta,x)\to\mathbb P(P<x)$ as $\delta\to0^+$.
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.7, p. 46.
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF.explanation: $\mathbb P(|P-x|\le\delta)\to\mathbb P(P=x)=0$ by continuity of measure along the decreasing sets, and `abs_smoothCDF_sub_le`.

MLMC.crossDiff_two.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §2.4 and Figure 2.1: in two dimensions $\boldsymbol\Delta P_{(\ell_1,\ell_2)}=P_{(\ell_1,\ell_2)}-P_{(\ell_1-1,\ell_2)}-P_{(\ell_1,\ell_2-1)}+P_{(\ell_1-1,\ell_2-1)}$
MLMC.crossDiff_two.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §2.4, pp. 12–13: Haji-Ali et al. "first define a backward difference operator in one particular dimension, $\Delta_dP_{\boldsymbol\ell}\equiv P_{\boldsymbol\ell}-P_{\boldsymbol\ell-\mathbf e_d}$ where $\mathbf e_d$ is the unit vector in direction $d$. They then define the cross-difference $\boldsymbol\Delta P_{\boldsymbol\ell}\equiv\big(\prod_{d=1}^D\Delta_d\big)P_{\boldsymbol\ell}$ … As an example, Figure 2.1 marks the four locations at which $P_{\boldsymbol\ell}$ must be computed to determine the value of $\boldsymbol\Delta P_{(5,4)}$ in the 2D application."

Let $P:\mathbb N^2\to\mathbb R$ be any function of the two-dimensional level $(\ell_1,\ell_2)$ and let $\boldsymbol\Delta P$ be its cross-difference (with $P$ read as $0$ at indices with a negative entry). Then for all $\ell_1,\ell_2\ge1$,
$$
\boldsymbol\Delta P_{(\ell_1,\ell_2)}=P_{(\ell_1,\ell_2)}-P_{(\ell_1-1,\ell_2)}-P_{(\ell_1,\ell_2-1)}+P_{(\ell_1-1,\ell_2-1)} ,
$$
the four evaluations at the corners of the unit square below $(\ell_1,\ell_2)$ that Figure 2.1 marks for $(\ell_1,\ell_2)=(5,4)$.

**Formalization Note** Multi-indices are functions `Fin 2 → ℕ`; the level $(a,b)$ is written `Fin.cons a (Fin.cons b e)` with `e : Fin 0 → ℕ` the empty tuple, and $\boldsymbol\Delta P$ is `crossDiff p`.
MLMC.crossDiff_two.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.4 (Multi-Index Monte Carlo), pp. 12–13 of the author's version, Figure 2.1; the cross-difference is due to A.-L. Haji-Ali, F. Nobile and R. Tempone (2014a), Multi Index Monte Carlo: when sparsity meets sampling, arXiv:1405.3757.
MLMC.crossDiff_two.explanation: Unfold the recursive definition twice: $\boldsymbol\Delta P_{(\ell_1,\ell_2)}$ is the one-dimensional difference in $\ell_2$ of $P_{(\ell_1,\cdot)}$ minus that of $P_{(\ell_1-1,\cdot)}$ (both present because $\ell_1,\ell_2\ne0$), and the four terms rearrange by ring arithmetic.

MLMC.randomised_optimal_cost.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §2.2: with the optimal $p_\ell$, $\sum V_\ell/p_\ell=(\sum\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell})(\sum\sqrt{V_\ell/C_\ell})$ and the cost is $\varepsilon^{-2}(\sum\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell})^2$
MLMC.randomised_optimal_cost.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §2.2, p. 10: "Provided $\beta>\gamma$, the optimal choice for $p_\ell$ is $p_\ell=\sqrt{V_\ell/C_\ell}\big(\sum_{\ell'=0}^\infty\sqrt{V_{\ell'}/C_{\ell'}}\big)^{-1}$. If $E_\ell^2\ll V_\ell$, then the condition that the variance of the estimator is approximately equal to $\varepsilon^2$ gives $N\approx\varepsilon^{-2}\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty V_\ell/p_\ell\approx\varepsilon^{-2}\big(\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell}\big)\big(\sum_{\ell'=0}^\infty\sqrt{V_{\ell'}/C_{\ell'}}\big)$ and therefore the total cost is $C=N\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty p_\ell C_\ell\approx\varepsilon^{-2}\big(\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell}\big)^2$."

Let $V_\ell,C_\ell>0$ ($\ell\in\mathbb N$) with $\sum_\ell\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell}<\infty$ and $Z=\sum_\ell\sqrt{V_\ell/C_\ell}<\infty$, let $p^\star_\ell=\sqrt{V_\ell/C_\ell}/Z$, and let $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$. Then
$$
\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\frac{V_\ell}{p^\star_\ell}=\Big(\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell}\Big)Z,\qquad \sum_{\ell=0}^\infty p^\star_\ell C_\ell=\frac{\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell}}{Z},
$$
$$
\varepsilon^{-2}\Big(\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\frac{V_\ell}{p^\star_\ell}\Big)\Big(\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty p^\star_\ell C_\ell\Big)=\varepsilon^{-2}\Big(\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell}\Big)^2 .
$$
So the paper's approximate equalities between the sums are exact; the approximations are only in neglecting $E_\ell^2$ in the variance and in rounding $N$ to an integer.

**Formalization Note** $p^\star$ is `optimalLevelProb V C`; the sums are `tsum`, and for $\varepsilon=0$ Lean's $0^{-1}=0$ makes the last identity $0=0$.
MLMC.randomised_optimal_cost.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.2 'Randomised MLMC for unbiased estimation', p. 10 of the author's version, presenting the single-term estimator of C.-H. Rhee and P. Glynn (2012, 2013).
MLMC.randomised_optimal_cost.explanation: With $Z=\sum_k\sqrt{V_k/C_k}$: $V_\ell/p^\star_\ell=Z\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell}$ and $p^\star_\ell C_\ell=\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell}/Z$ termwise, so the two sums are $Z\sum_\ell\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell}$ and $\sum_\ell\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell}/Z$; the product identity is `randomised_optimal_p_eq`.

MLMC.subsetCost_eq.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §2.6: the cost of MLMC on the levels $\ell_0<\dots<\ell_M$ is $\varepsilon^{-2}(\sqrt{V_{\ell_0}C_{\ell_0}}+\sum_{m=1}^M\sqrt{V_{\ell_{m-1},\ell_m}C_{\ell_{m-1},\ell_m}})^2$
MLMC.subsetCost_eq.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §2.6, p. 18: "Suppose that one starts with a large collection of potential levels; how does one decide which subset to use? One approach … is to first use a number of trial samples to obtain an estimate of $V_\ell=\mathbb V[P_\ell]$ and $V_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\equiv\mathbb V[P_{\ell_2}-P_{\ell_1}]$ for all pairs $(\ell_1,\ell_2)$, with $\ell_1<\ell_2$, with associated costs $C_\ell$ and $C_{\ell_1,\ell_2}$. For a particular ordered subset of levels, $\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M\}$, with fixed $\ell_M=L$ to achieve a user-specified accuracy, following the analysis in Section 1.3 which led to (1.1), we obtain the cost $C(\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M)=\varepsilon^{-2}\big(\sqrt{V_{\ell_0}C_{\ell_0}}+\sum_{m=1}^M\sqrt{V_{\ell_m,\ell_{m-1}}C_{\ell_m,\ell_{m-1}}}\big)^2$. If the maximum number of levels is not too large, it is possible to perform an exhaustive search to find the optimal subset $\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M\}$ which minimises this cost."

Let $M\in\mathbb N$ and let $\ell_0<\ell_1<\dots<\ell_M$ be natural numbers (the levels used). Let $V,C:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$, $V_2,C_2:\mathbb N\times\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ (with $V_\ell=V(\ell)$, $V_{\ell_1,\ell_2}=V_2(\ell_1,\ell_2)$, and similarly for the costs) and $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$. Then the cost $\mathrm{subsetCost}$ of MLMC on the set $s=\{\ell_0,\dots,\ell_M\}$ is
$$
\mathrm{subsetCost}(V,C,V_2,C_2,\varepsilon,s)=\varepsilon^{-2}\Big(\sqrt{V_{\ell_0}C_{\ell_0}}+\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sqrt{V_{\ell_{m-1},\ell_m}C_{\ell_{m-1},\ell_m}}\Big)^2 ,
$$
the formula of the paper. (The paper writes the pair as $V_{\ell_m,\ell_{m-1}}$; by its definition $V_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\equiv\mathbb V[P_{\ell_2}-P_{\ell_1}]$ for $\ell_1<\ell_2$, the variance of the correction $P_{\ell_m}-P_{\ell_{m-1}}$ is $V_{\ell_{m-1},\ell_m}$. The paper also names the subset $\{\ell_1,\dots,\ell_M\}$ while its formula starts at $\ell_0$.) That this is the least cost for variance $\varepsilon^2$ is `subset_optimal_cost`.

**Formalization Note** The levels are a strictly increasing map `ℓ : Fin (M + 1) → ℕ` and $s$ is its image `Finset.univ.image ℓ`; the index $m\in\{1,\dots,M\}$ is `m.succ` for `m : Fin M`, and $m-1$ is `m.castSucc`.
MLMC.subsetCost_eq.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.6 (Non-geometric MLMC), p. 18 of the author's version, after F. Vidal-Codina, N.C. Nguyen, M.B. Giles and J. Peraire (2014).
MLMC.subsetCost_eq.explanation: The map $m\mapsto\ell_m$ is injective, so the sum over $s$ is a sum over $m=0,\dots,M$; split off $m=0$. The smallest level $\ell_0$ has no level of $s$ below it, so its correction carries $V_{\ell_0},C_{\ell_0}$; for $m\ge1$ the levels of $s$ below $\ell_m$ are $\ell_0,\dots,\ell_{m-1}$ (strict monotonicity), whose maximum is $\ell_{m-1}$.

MLMC.sum_subsetCorr.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §2.6: the corrections of MLMC on a subset of the levels telescope to $P$ at the finest level of the subset
MLMC.sum_subsetCorr.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §2.6, p. 18: "Suppose that one starts with a large collection of potential levels; how does one decide which subset to use? One approach … is to first use a number of trial samples to obtain an estimate of $V_\ell=\mathbb V[P_\ell]$ and $V_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\equiv\mathbb V[P_{\ell_2}-P_{\ell_1}]$ for all pairs $(\ell_1,\ell_2)$, with $\ell_1<\ell_2$, with associated costs $C_\ell$ and $C_{\ell_1,\ell_2}$. For a particular ordered subset of levels, $\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M\}$, with fixed $\ell_M=L$ to achieve a user-specified accuracy, following the analysis in Section 1.3 which led to (1.1), we obtain the cost $C(\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M)=\varepsilon^{-2}\big(\sqrt{V_{\ell_0}C_{\ell_0}}+\sum_{m=1}^M\sqrt{V_{\ell_m,\ell_{m-1}}C_{\ell_m,\ell_{m-1}}}\big)^2$. If the maximum number of levels is not too large, it is possible to perform an exhaustive search to find the optimal subset $\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M\}$ which minimises this cost."

Let $p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ (for instance $p(\ell)=\mathbb E[P_\ell]$, or the value of $P_\ell$ at a fixed outcome) and let $s\subseteq\mathbb N$ be a finite nonempty set of levels, $\ell_0<\ell_1<\dots<\ell_M$. MLMC on the levels of $s$ uses the corrections $P_{\ell_0}$ and $P_{\ell_m}-P_{\ell_{m-1}}$ ($1\le m\le M$); in the notation of the definition $\mathrm{subsetCorr}$ these are $\mathrm{subsetCorr}(p,\,(i,j)\mapsto p(j)-p(i),\,s,\,\ell)$ for $\ell\in s$. Then
$$
\sum_{\ell\in s}\mathrm{subsetCorr}\big(p,\,(i,j)\mapsto p(j)-p(i),\,s,\,\ell\big)=p(\max s),
$$
that is $p(\ell_0)+\sum_{m=1}^M\big(p(\ell_m)-p(\ell_{m-1})\big)=p(\ell_M)$. With $\ell_M=L$ fixed, as in the paper, MLMC on any subset has the expectation $\mathbb E[P_L]$, and so the same bias as MLMC on all the levels up to $L$; only the cost depends on the subset.
MLMC.sum_subsetCorr.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.6 (Non-geometric MLMC), p. 18 of the author's version.
MLMC.sum_subsetCorr.explanation: Induction over $s$ by adding a new largest element $a$ to a set $t$ whose elements are all below $a$: the levels of $t$ keep their predecessors, $a$ has predecessor $\max t$ (or none if $t=\emptyset$), so the sum becomes $p(a)-p(\max t)+p(\max t)=p(a)$ (or $p(a)$), and $\max(t\cup\{a\})=a$.

MLMC.subset_optimal_cost.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §2.6: MLMC on a subset of the levels has least cost $\mathrm{subsetCost}$ for variance $\varepsilon^2$, by (1.1)
MLMC.subset_optimal_cost.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §2.6, p. 18: "Suppose that one starts with a large collection of potential levels; how does one decide which subset to use? One approach … is to first use a number of trial samples to obtain an estimate of $V_\ell=\mathbb V[P_\ell]$ and $V_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\equiv\mathbb V[P_{\ell_2}-P_{\ell_1}]$ for all pairs $(\ell_1,\ell_2)$, with $\ell_1<\ell_2$, with associated costs $C_\ell$ and $C_{\ell_1,\ell_2}$. For a particular ordered subset of levels, $\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M\}$, with fixed $\ell_M=L$ to achieve a user-specified accuracy, following the analysis in Section 1.3 which led to (1.1), we obtain the cost $C(\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M)=\varepsilon^{-2}\big(\sqrt{V_{\ell_0}C_{\ell_0}}+\sum_{m=1}^M\sqrt{V_{\ell_m,\ell_{m-1}}C_{\ell_m,\ell_{m-1}}}\big)^2$. If the maximum number of levels is not too large, it is possible to perform an exhaustive search to find the optimal subset $\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M\}$ which minimises this cost."

Let $V,C:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ and $V_2,C_2:\mathbb N\times\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be positive (variances and costs as above), $\varepsilon>0$, and let $s\subseteq\mathbb N$ be a finite nonempty set of levels. On a level $\ell\in s$ MLMC on the levels of $s$ samples the correction with variance $W_\ell=\mathrm{subsetCorr}(V,V_2,s,\ell)$ and cost $K_\ell=\mathrm{subsetCorr}(C,C_2,s,\ell)$ ($V_{\ell_0},C_{\ell_0}$ on the smallest level, $V_{\ell_{m-1},\ell_m},C_{\ell_{m-1},\ell_m}$ on the others). Then the least total cost $\sum_{\ell\in s}N_\ell K_\ell$ over all real sample numbers $N_\ell>0$ ($\ell\in s$) with total variance $\sum_{\ell\in s}W_\ell/N_\ell\le\varepsilon^2$ exists and equals
$$
\mathrm{subsetCost}(V,C,V_2,C_2,\varepsilon,s)=\varepsilon^{-2}\Big(\sum_{\ell\in s}\sqrt{W_\ell K_\ell}\Big)^2,
$$
which is the formula of the paper (`subsetCost_eq`).

**Formalization Note** The minimum is Lean's `IsLeast` on the set of costs $\{\sum_{\ell\in s}N_\ell K_\ell\}$ of the admissible allocations $N:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$; as in (1.1), sample numbers are real.
MLMC.subset_optimal_cost.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.6 (Non-geometric MLMC), p. 18 of the author's version, with the optimal allocation of §1.3, eq. (1.1).
MLMC.subset_optimal_cost.explanation: This is the optimal-allocation result (1.1), `optimal_cost_isLeast`, for the finite index set $s$ with variances $W_\ell$ and costs $K_\ell$, which are positive because both branches of $\mathrm{subsetCorr}$ are.

MLMC.card_levelSubsets.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §2.6: the subsets of $\{0,\dots,L\}$ that keep the finest level $L$ number $2^L$
MLMC.card_levelSubsets.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §2.6, p. 18: "Suppose that one starts with a large collection of potential levels; how does one decide which subset to use? One approach … is to first use a number of trial samples to obtain an estimate of $V_\ell=\mathbb V[P_\ell]$ and $V_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\equiv\mathbb V[P_{\ell_2}-P_{\ell_1}]$ for all pairs $(\ell_1,\ell_2)$, with $\ell_1<\ell_2$, with associated costs $C_\ell$ and $C_{\ell_1,\ell_2}$. For a particular ordered subset of levels, $\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M\}$, with fixed $\ell_M=L$ to achieve a user-specified accuracy, following the analysis in Section 1.3 which led to (1.1), we obtain the cost $C(\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M)=\varepsilon^{-2}\big(\sqrt{V_{\ell_0}C_{\ell_0}}+\sum_{m=1}^M\sqrt{V_{\ell_m,\ell_{m-1}}C_{\ell_m,\ell_{m-1}}}\big)^2$. If the maximum number of levels is not too large, it is possible to perform an exhaustive search to find the optimal subset $\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M\}$ which minimises this cost."

For every $L\in\mathbb N$, the number of subsets $s\subseteq\{0,1,\dots,L\}$ with $L\in s$ is $2^L$. These are the candidate subsets of the exhaustive search (`exists_optimal_subset`), so its size is $2^L$ evaluations of the cost formula.
MLMC.card_levelSubsets.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.6 (Non-geometric MLMC), p. 18 of the author's version.
MLMC.card_levelSubsets.explanation: The map $t\mapsto t\cup\{L\}$ is a bijection from the subsets of $\{0,\dots,L-1\}$ onto the subsets of $\{0,\dots,L\}$ containing $L$ (its inverse removes $L$), and $\{0,\dots,L-1\}$ has $2^L$ subsets.

MLMC.exists_optimal_subset.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §2.6: the exhaustive search over the subsets of $\{0,\dots,L\}$ containing $L$ finds a subset of least cost
MLMC.exists_optimal_subset.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §2.6, p. 18: "Suppose that one starts with a large collection of potential levels; how does one decide which subset to use? One approach … is to first use a number of trial samples to obtain an estimate of $V_\ell=\mathbb V[P_\ell]$ and $V_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\equiv\mathbb V[P_{\ell_2}-P_{\ell_1}]$ for all pairs $(\ell_1,\ell_2)$, with $\ell_1<\ell_2$, with associated costs $C_\ell$ and $C_{\ell_1,\ell_2}$. For a particular ordered subset of levels, $\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M\}$, with fixed $\ell_M=L$ to achieve a user-specified accuracy, following the analysis in Section 1.3 which led to (1.1), we obtain the cost $C(\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M)=\varepsilon^{-2}\big(\sqrt{V_{\ell_0}C_{\ell_0}}+\sum_{m=1}^M\sqrt{V_{\ell_m,\ell_{m-1}}C_{\ell_m,\ell_{m-1}}}\big)^2$. If the maximum number of levels is not too large, it is possible to perform an exhaustive search to find the optimal subset $\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\dots,\ell_M\}$ which minimises this cost."

Let $V,C:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$, $V_2,C_2:\mathbb N\times\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$ and $L\in\mathbb N$. Among the subsets $s\subseteq\{0,\dots,L\}$ with $L\in s$ there is one, $s^\star$, with
$$
\mathrm{subsetCost}(V,C,V_2,C_2,\varepsilon,s^\star)\le\mathrm{subsetCost}(V,C,V_2,C_2,\varepsilon,t)\quad\text{for every subset }t\subseteq\{0,\dots,L\}\text{ with }L\in t .
$$
In particular $s^\star$ costs no more than standard MLMC on all the levels $\{0,\dots,L\}$. There are $2^L$ candidates (`card_levelSubsets`).
MLMC.exists_optimal_subset.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §2.6 (Non-geometric MLMC), p. 18 of the author's version.
MLMC.exists_optimal_subset.explanation: The candidates form a finite set, nonempty because it contains $\{L\}$; a real function on a finite nonempty set attains its minimum.

MLMC.mlqmc_inner_terminates.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §3.5, Algorithm 2: the greedy doubling (3.3) reaches any variance target $\sum_{\ell\le L}V_\ell\le\theta$ in finitely many steps
MLMC.mlqmc_inner_terminates.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §3.5, p. 27: "Since $V_\ell$ is now defined to be the variance of the average, for a given number of levels $L$, the aim is to choose the $N_\ell$ in a way which ensures that $\sum_{\ell=0}^LV_\ell\le\frac12\varepsilon^2$. (3.2) … Doubling $N_\ell$ will usually eliminate a large fraction of the variance, so the greatest reduction in total variance relative to the additional computational effort is achieved by doubling $N_\ell$ on the level $\ell^*=\arg\max_\ell V_\ell/(N_\ell C_\ell)$. (3.3) Based on this, and using the same test for weak convergence as in the MLMC algorithm, the MLQMC algorithm is: **Algorithm 2** start with $L=2$, and an initial set size $N_\ell=1$ on levels $\ell=0,1,2$; while not converged do: evaluate 32 set averages on any level with new/changed values of $N_\ell$; compute corresponding new/changed estimates for $V_\ell$; test whether total variance condition (3.2) is satisfied; if total variance still too big then determine $\ell^*$ defined by (3.3) and double $N_{\ell^*}$, else test for weak convergence, and if not converged set $L:=L+1$, and initialise $N_L=1$."

As for Algorithm 1, the algorithm is analysed with exact values. After $k$ doublings on level $\ell$ the set size is $N_\ell=2^k$, and $v(\ell,k)$ denotes the variance $V_\ell$ of the level-$\ell$ average after $k$ doublings. The ratio of (3.3) is $r(\ell,k)=v(\ell,k)/(2^kC_\ell)$. How fast $v(\ell,k)$ decays is a matter of QMC theory and is not assumed; only $v(\ell,k)>0$ and $v(\ell,k)\to0$ as $k\to\infty$ on each level are.

Let $v:\mathbb N\times\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ with $v(\ell,k)>0$ for all $\ell,k$ and $v(\ell,k)\to0$ as $k\to\infty$ for each $\ell$, and let $C_\ell>0$. Fix the finest level $L$ and any starting numbers of doublings $k^{(0)}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$. The inner loop replaces $k$ by $k+\mathbf e_{\ell^*}$, where $\ell^*\in\{0,\dots,L\}$ maximises $r(\ell,k_\ell)$ over $\ell\le L$ (ties broken arbitrarily); let $k^{(n)}$ be the numbers of doublings after $n$ passes. Then for every $\theta>0$ there is $n$ with
$$
\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}v\big(\ell,k^{(n)}_\ell\big)\le\theta ,
$$
so the inner loop of Algorithm 2 (with $\theta=\varepsilon^2/2$, (3.2)) terminates.

**Formalization Note** $\ell^*$ is `mlqmcLevel v C L k` (a maximiser chosen by `Classical.choose`), one pass is `mlqmcStep` and $k^{(n)}$ is `mlqmcIter v C L k₀ n`.
MLMC.mlqmc_inner_terminates.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §3.5 (MLQMC), eqs. (3.2)–(3.3) and Algorithm 2, p. 27 of the author's version.
MLMC.mlqmc_inner_terminates.explanation: Choose $K$ such that $v(\ell,k)\le\theta/(L+1)$ for all $\ell\le L$ and $k\ge K$, let $\eta>0$ be the least ratio $r(\ell,k)$ over $\ell\le L$, $k<K$, and choose $K'$ such that $r(\ell,k)<\eta$ for $k\ge K'$. While some level has fewer than $K$ doublings, the level doubled has fewer than $K'$ (otherwise its ratio would be below that level's), so every level stays below $B=K'+\sum_\ell k^{(0)}_\ell$. Each pass adds one doubling, so after $(L+1)B+1$ passes every level has at least $K$ doublings and the total variance is at most $\theta$.

MLMC.mlqmc_algorithm.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §3.5, Algorithm 2 (exact values): MLQMC stops at the level of the Algorithm 1 test, with $\sum_{\ell\le L}V_\ell\le\varepsilon^2/2$
MLMC.mlqmc_algorithm.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §3.5, p. 27: "Since $V_\ell$ is now defined to be the variance of the average, for a given number of levels $L$, the aim is to choose the $N_\ell$ in a way which ensures that $\sum_{\ell=0}^LV_\ell\le\frac12\varepsilon^2$. (3.2) … Doubling $N_\ell$ will usually eliminate a large fraction of the variance, so the greatest reduction in total variance relative to the additional computational effort is achieved by doubling $N_\ell$ on the level $\ell^*=\arg\max_\ell V_\ell/(N_\ell C_\ell)$. (3.3) Based on this, and using the same test for weak convergence as in the MLMC algorithm, the MLQMC algorithm is: **Algorithm 2** start with $L=2$, and an initial set size $N_\ell=1$ on levels $\ell=0,1,2$; while not converged do: evaluate 32 set averages on any level with new/changed values of $N_\ell$; compute corresponding new/changed estimates for $V_\ell$; test whether total variance condition (3.2) is satisfied; if total variance still too big then determine $\ell^*$ defined by (3.3) and double $N_{\ell^*}$, else test for weak convergence, and if not converged set $L:=L+1$, and initialise $N_L=1$."

As for Algorithm 1, the algorithm is analysed with exact values. After $k$ doublings on level $\ell$ the set size is $N_\ell=2^k$, and $v(\ell,k)$ denotes the variance $V_\ell$ of the level-$\ell$ average after $k$ doublings. The ratio of (3.3) is $r(\ell,k)=v(\ell,k)/(2^kC_\ell)$. How fast $v(\ell,k)$ decays is a matter of QMC theory and is not assumed; only $v(\ell,k)>0$ and $v(\ell,k)\to0$ as $k\to\infty$ on each level are.

The state when Algorithm 2 leaves its inner loop with finest level $L\ge2$ is $\mathrm{mlqmcState}(L)$: the inner loop (greedy doubling until $\sum_{\ell\le L}V_\ell\le\varepsilon^2/2$) is run from $N_\ell=1$ at $L=2$, and again after each new level is added with $N_L=1$. The weak-convergence test is that of Algorithm 1: with the exact means $m_\ell=\mathbb E[P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}]$ it passes at $L$ when $\max(|m_L|,2^{-\alpha}|m_{L-1}|,2^{-2\alpha}|m_{L-2}|)/(2^\alpha-1)\le\varepsilon/\sqrt2$, and the outer loop stops at the least such $L\ge2$, $L^\star=\mathrm{alg1Level}(m,\alpha,\varepsilon)$.

Let $m_\ell\to0$, $\alpha,\varepsilon>0$, $C_\ell>0$, and let $v(\ell,k)>0$ with $v(\ell,k)\to0$ as $k\to\infty$ for each $\ell$. Then $L^\star\ge2$, the test passes at $L^\star$, every inner loop terminates, and at exit
$$
\sum_{\ell=0}^{L^\star}v\big(\ell,k_\ell\big)\le\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2},\qquad k=\mathrm{mlqmcState}(L^\star),
$$
the variance condition (3.2).
MLMC.mlqmc_algorithm.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §3.5 (MLQMC), eqs. (3.2)–(3.3) and Algorithm 2, p. 27 of the author's version; the weak-convergence test of §3.1 (Algorithm 1).
MLMC.mlqmc_algorithm.explanation: `alg1_terminates` gives a level $L\ge2$ that passes the test, so $L^\star$ is defined and passes it (`alg1Level_spec`). At every $L\ge2$ the state is the result of an inner loop, which terminates by `mlqmc_inner_terminates`, so the first iterate meeting the target exists and the total variance there is at most $\varepsilon^2/2$.

MLMC.mlqmc_mse.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §3.5, Algorithm 2 (exact values): at exit the MLQMC estimator has mean square error at most $\varepsilon^2$
MLMC.mlqmc_mse.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §3.5, p. 27: "Since $V_\ell$ is now defined to be the variance of the average, for a given number of levels $L$, the aim is to choose the $N_\ell$ in a way which ensures that $\sum_{\ell=0}^LV_\ell\le\frac12\varepsilon^2$. (3.2) … Doubling $N_\ell$ will usually eliminate a large fraction of the variance, so the greatest reduction in total variance relative to the additional computational effort is achieved by doubling $N_\ell$ on the level $\ell^*=\arg\max_\ell V_\ell/(N_\ell C_\ell)$. (3.3) Based on this, and using the same test for weak convergence as in the MLMC algorithm, the MLQMC algorithm is: **Algorithm 2** start with $L=2$, and an initial set size $N_\ell=1$ on levels $\ell=0,1,2$; while not converged do: evaluate 32 set averages on any level with new/changed values of $N_\ell$; compute corresponding new/changed estimates for $V_\ell$; test whether total variance condition (3.2) is satisfied; if total variance still too big then determine $\ell^*$ defined by (3.3) and double $N_{\ell^*}$, else test for weak convergence, and if not converged set $L:=L+1$, and initialise $N_L=1$."

As for Algorithm 1, the algorithm is analysed with exact values. After $k$ doublings on level $\ell$ the set size is $N_\ell=2^k$, and $v(\ell,k)$ denotes the variance $V_\ell$ of the level-$\ell$ average after $k$ doublings. The ratio of (3.3) is $r(\ell,k)=v(\ell,k)/(2^kC_\ell)$. How fast $v(\ell,k)$ decays is a matter of QMC theory and is not assumed; only $v(\ell,k)>0$ and $v(\ell,k)\to0$ as $k\to\infty$ on each level are.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $P_0,P_1,\dots:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable with $\mathbb E[P_\ell]\to\mathbb E[P]$, and $m_\ell=\mathbb E[P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}]$ ($P_{-1}=0$), so that $m_\ell\to0$. Let $\alpha,\varepsilon>0$, $C_\ell>0$ and $v$ as above ($v(\ell,k)>0$, $v(\ell,k)\to0$ as $k\to\infty$), and let $L^\star=\mathrm{alg1Level}(m,\alpha,\varepsilon)$ be the level at which Algorithm 2 stops. Suppose that for some $k\le2$ the corrections beyond $L^\star$ decay at least geometrically from the anchor $L^\star-k$: $|m_\ell|\le|m_{L^\star-k}|\,2^{-\alpha(\ell-(L^\star-k))}$ for all $\ell>L^\star$. Let $Y$ be square-integrable with $\mathbb E[Y]=\mathbb E[P_{L^\star}]$ and variance at most the total variance at exit, $\mathbb V[Y]\le\sum_{\ell\le L^\star}v(\ell,k_\ell)$ with $k=\mathrm{mlqmcState}(L^\star)$ (the MLQMC estimator, the sum of independent level averages). Then
$$
\mathbb E\big[(Y-\mathbb E[P])^2\big]\le\varepsilon^2 .
$$
MLMC.mlqmc_mse.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §3.5 (MLQMC), eq. (3.2) and Algorithm 2, p. 27 of the author's version; the MSE split and weak-convergence test of §3.1.
MLMC.mlqmc_mse.explanation: Since $\mathbb E[P_\ell]$ converges, $m_{\ell+1}=\mathbb E[P_{\ell+1}]-\mathbb E[P_\ell]\to0$. By `mlqmc_algorithm` the variance at exit is at most $\varepsilon^2/2$ and the test passes at $L^\star$; the rest is `alg1_mse`: the robust test and the geometric decay bound the bias by $\varepsilon/\sqrt2$, and MSE $=$ variance $+$ bias$^2$.

MLMC.tendsto_kernel_integral_signed.theorem_title: Rescaled kernels $c\,g(c(x-\cdot))$ with $g$ continuous, $g=0$ off $[-1,1]$, $\int g=1$ form an approximate identity (Giles (2015), §5.7)
MLMC.tendsto_kernel_integral_signed.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "The same paper also discusses the extension to density estimation. In this case, the density $\rho(x)$ of the scalar output $P$ is given by $\rho(x)=\lim_{\delta\to0}\mathbb E\big[\delta^{-1}g((x-P)/\delta)\big]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $|x|>1$, and $\int_{-1}^1g(x)\,dx=1$. This has similarities with kernel density estimation (Silverman 1986) …"

This is the analytic core of the density limit. Let $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $g(y)=0$ whenever $|y|>1$, and $\int_{\mathbb R}g(y)\,dy=1$ ($g$ may take negative values). Let $r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Lebesgue integrable and continuous at the point $x$. Then
$$
\lim_{c\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb R}c\,g\big(c(x-y)\big)\,r(y)\,dy=r(x).
$$
With $c=\delta^{-1}$ this is $\int\delta^{-1}g((x-y)/\delta)\,r(y)\,dy\to r(x)$ as $\delta\to0^+$.
MLMC.tendsto_kernel_integral_signed.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.7 (CDF and density estimation), p. 46 of the author's version; see also B.W. Silverman, Density Estimation for Statistics and Data Analysis (1986).
MLMC.tendsto_kernel_integral_signed.explanation: With $A=\int|g|\ge|\int g|=1$, the functions $\varphi_1=(2|g|+g)/(2A+1)$ and $\varphi_2=(2|g|-g)/(2A-1)$ are nonnegative, vanish off $[-1,1]$ and have integral $1$, and $g=\big((2A+1)\varphi_1-(2A-1)\varphi_2\big)/2$. For each $\varphi_i$ the claim is Mathlib's peak-function theorem `tendsto_integral_comp_smul_smul_of_integrable'` (its decay condition holds because $\varphi_i$ has compact support), and the integrands are integrable because $\varphi_i$ is bounded and $r$ integrable; the limit of the combination is $\big((2A+1)-(2A-1)\big)r(x)/2=r(x)$.

MLMC.tendsto_density.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.7: $\rho(x)=\lim_{\delta\to0}\mathbb E[\delta^{-1}g((x-P)/\delta)]$ when $P$ has a density continuous at $x$
MLMC.tendsto_density.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "The same paper also discusses the extension to density estimation. In this case, the density $\rho(x)$ of the scalar output $P$ is given by $\rho(x)=\lim_{\delta\to0}\mathbb E\big[\delta^{-1}g((x-P)/\delta)\big]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $|x|>1$, and $\int_{-1}^1g(x)\,dx=1$. This has similarities with kernel density estimation (Silverman 1986) …"

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and $P:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ measurable, and suppose the law of $P$ has a density $\rho:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ (measurable) with respect to Lebesgue measure: $\mathbb P(P\in B)=\int_B\rho(y)\,dy$ for Borel $B$. Let $x\in\mathbb R$ be a point at which $\rho$ is continuous, and let $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with $g(y)=0$ for $|y|>1$ and $\int_{\mathbb R}g(y)\,dy=1$. Then
$$
\lim_{\delta\to0^+}\mathbb E\Big[\delta^{-1}g\Big(\frac{x-P}{\delta}\Big)\Big]=\rho(x).
$$

**Formalization Note** The density is `ρ : ℝ → ℝ≥0` with `μ.map P = volume.withDensity (fun y => (ρ y : ℝ≥0∞))`; the limit is along `𝓝[>] 0`, i.e. $\delta\to0$ through positive values.
MLMC.tendsto_density.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.7 (CDF and density estimation), p. 46 of the author's version (after M.B. Giles, T. Nagapetyan and K. Ritter (2014), multilevel CDF and density estimation).
MLMC.tendsto_density.explanation: Since $\int\rho=\mathbb P(\Omega)=1$, $\rho$ is integrable. By the change of variables to the law of $P$ and then to its density, $\mathbb E[\delta^{-1}g((x-P)/\delta)]=\int\delta^{-1}g(\delta^{-1}(x-y))\rho(y)\,dy$, and `tendsto_kernel_integral_signed` with $c=\delta^{-1}\to\infty$ as $\delta\to0^+$ gives the limit $\rho(x)$.

MLMC.splitting_mean_variance.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.2, splitting: averaging $M$ sub-samples keeps the mean of the conditional expectation and adds the variance $\mathbb E[v]/M$
MLMC.splitting_mean_variance.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.2, pp. 36–38: "The conditional expectation technique works well in 1D where there is a known analytic value for the conditional expectation, but in multiple dimensions it may not be known. In this case, one can use the technique of “splitting” (Asmussen and Glynn 2007). Here the conditional expectation is replaced by a numerical estimate, averaging over a number of sub-samples. i.e. for each set of Brownian increments up to one fine timestep before the end, one uses a number of samples of the final Brownian increment to produce an average payoff. If the number of sub-samples is chosen appropriately, the variance is the same, to leading order, without any increase in the computational cost, again to leading order."

Let $(\Omega_1,\mu)$ and $(\Omega_2,\nu)$ be probability spaces: $x\sim\mu$ is the outer sample (the Brownian increments up to one fine timestep before the end) and $z\sim\nu$ one sample of the final increment. Let $g:\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $\int g^2\,d(\mu\otimes\nu)<\infty$, and write
$$
m(x)=\int g(x,z)\,d\nu(z),\qquad v(x)=\int\big(g(x,z)-m(x)\big)^2\,d\nu(z)
$$
for the conditional mean (the conditional expectation that splitting replaces) and the conditional variance. On the product space $\Omega_1\times\Omega_2^{\mathbb N}$ with the measure $\mu\otimes\nu^{\otimes\mathbb N}$ (an outer sample and independent sub-samples $z_0,z_1,\dots$), let $M\ge1$ and
$$
S(x,z)=\frac1M\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}g(x,z_j)
$$
be the splitting estimator. Then
$$
\mathbb E[S]=\int m\,d\mu,\qquad \mathbb V[S]=\mathbb V_\mu[m]+\frac1M\int v\,d\mu .
$$
So splitting has the same mean as the exact conditional expectation $m(x)$ and adds the variance $\mathbb E[v]/M$, which vanishes as $M\to\infty$; the "to leading order" of the paper refers to choosing $M$ large enough that this term is negligible while the extra cost of $M$ final steps is small.

**Formalization Note** The product measure on $\Omega_2^{\mathbb N}$ is Mathlib's `Measure.infinitePi (fun _ => ν)`; only the first $M$ coordinates are used. $\mathbb V$ is Mathlib's `variance`.
MLMC.splitting_mean_variance.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.2 (Milstein discretisation; digital options), pp. 36–38 of the author's version; splitting after S. Asmussen and P. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation (2007).
MLMC.splitting_mean_variance.explanation:
Each map $(x,z)\mapsto(x,z_j)$ pushes $\mu\otimes
u^{\otimes\mathbb N}$ forward to $\mu\otimes
u$, and for $j
e k$ the map $(x,z)\mapsto(x,(z_j,z_k))$ pushes it to $\mu\otimes(
u\otimes
u)$. Hence $\mathbb E[g(x,z_j)]=\int m$, $\mathbb E[g(x,z_j)^2]=\int\!\!\int g^2$ and, by Fubini and $\int g(x,a)g(x,b)\,d(
u\otimes
u)=m(x)^2$, $\mathbb E[g(x,z_j)g(x,z_k)]=\int m^2$. Expanding the square, $\mathbb E[S^2]= ig(M\!\int\!\!\int g^2+M(M-1)\int m^2 ig)/M^2$. For $\mu$-a.e. $x$, $g(x,\cdot)\in L^2(
u)$ and $v(x)=\int g(x,\cdot)^2-m(x)^2\ge0$, so $m\in L^2(\mu)$ and $\int v=\int\!\!\int g^2-\int m^2$; the variances are $\mathbb E[\cdot^2]-\mathbb E[\cdot]^2$.

MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledIncr_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §8: one coupled fine step changes the difference $d$ of the paths to $d+I_a-I_b$ with $\mathbb E[(d+I_a-I_b)^2]\le d^2+2|d||a-b|+|a-b|+|a-b|^2$
MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledIncr_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §8, p. 55: "the first step is to express the coarse path Poisson variate as the sum of two Poisson variates, $P(h\lambda(x^c_n))$ corresponding to the first and second fine path timesteps. For the first of the two fine timesteps, the coarse and fine path Poisson variates are coupled by defining two Poisson variates based on the minimum of the two reactions rates, and the absolute difference, $P_1=P\big(h\min(\lambda(x_n),\lambda(x^c_n))\big)$, $P_2=P\big(h|\lambda(x_n)-\lambda(x^c_n)|\big)$, and then using $P_1$ as the Poisson variate for the path with the smaller rate, and $P_1+P_2$ for the path with the larger rate."

For all rates $a,b\ge0$ and states $x,y\in\mathbb N$, under the law of the coupled increments $(I_a,I_b)$ (`coupledIncr`),
$$
\mathbb E\big[(x+I_a-(y+I_b))^2\big]\le(x-y)^2+2|x-y|\,|a-b|+|a-b|+|a-b|^2 ,
$$
the expectation being the lower integral of the nonnegative square.
MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledIncr_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §8, pp. 55–56 (after D.F. Anderson and D.J. Higham, Multilevel Monte Carlo for continuous time Markov chains, with applications in biochemical kinetics, Multiscale Model. Simul. 10 (2012) 146–179).
MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledIncr_le.explanation: For every outcome $|I_a-I_b|\le P_2$, so $(d+I_a-I_b)^2\le d^2+2|d|P_2+P_2^2$ with $d=x-y$. Integrate: $P_2\sim\mathrm{Po}(|a-b|)$ is the second factor of the product law, with $\mathbb E P_2=|a-b|$ and $\mathbb E P_2^2=|a-b|+|a-b|^2$ (`lintegral_poly_poissonMeasure`).

MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledTwoStep_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §8: over one coarse step (two coupled fine steps) the mean square difference of the paths grows by a factor $1+O(h)$ and an additive $O(h^2)$
MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledTwoStep_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §8, p. 55: "the first step is to express the coarse path Poisson variate as the sum of two Poisson variates, $P(h\lambda(x^c_n))$ corresponding to the first and second fine path timesteps. For the first of the two fine timesteps, the coarse and fine path Poisson variates are coupled by defining two Poisson variates based on the minimum of the two reactions rates, and the absolute difference, $P_1=P\big(h\min(\lambda(x_n),\lambda(x^c_n))\big)$, $P_2=P\big(h|\lambda(x_n)-\lambda(x^c_n)|\big)$, and then using $P_1$ as the Poisson variate for the path with the smaller rate, and $P_1+P_2$ for the path with the larger rate."

Let $\lambda:\mathbb N\to[0,\infty)$ be the propensity function and $h\ge0$ the fine time step. In the coupled simulation (`coupledChain`) both paths start at $x_0$, and each coarse step of size $2h$ is made of two fine steps (`coupledTwoStep`): in each, the fine increment, of rate $h\lambda(x)$ at the current fine state $x$, is coupled (`coupledIncr`) with one half of the coarse increment, of rate $h\lambda(x^c)$ at the coarse state $x^c$ at the start of the coarse step. Expectations of nonnegative quantities are lower integrals. Let $\kappa\ge0$ and $\ell\in\mathbb R$ be such that the scaled rates satisfy $|h\lambda(x)-h\lambda(y)|\le\kappa|x-y|$ and $h\lambda(y)\le\ell$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb N$ (for a $K$-Lipschitz propensity bounded by $\Lambda$: $\kappa=hK$, $\ell=h\Lambda$). Then from every pair of states $(x,x^c)$, after the two coupled fine steps,
$$
\mathbb E\big[(x_2-x^c_2)^2\big]\le(1+4\kappa+2\kappa^2)^2(x-x^c)^2+(\kappa+2\kappa^2)(\ell+\ell^2)+\kappa\ell .
$$
With $\kappa=hK$ and $\ell=h\Lambda$ the factor is $1+O(h)$ and the additive term $O(h^2)$.
MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledTwoStep_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §8, pp. 55–56 (after D.F. Anderson and D.J. Higham, Multilevel Monte Carlo for continuous time Markov chains, with applications in biochemical kinetics, Multiscale Model. Simul. 10 (2012) 146–179).
MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledTwoStep_le.explanation: Let $d_1$ be the difference after the first fine step and $j$ the first half of the coarse increment. In the second fine step the rates are $h\lambda(x+i)$ and $h\lambda(x^c)$, whose difference is at most $\kappa|x+i-x^c|\le\kappa(|d_1|+j)$. By `lintegral_sq_coupledIncr_le` and $|d_1|\le d_1^2$ (integers, `abs_natCast_sub_le_sq`), the second step gives at most $(1+4\kappa+2\kappa^2)d_1^2+(\kappa+2\kappa^2)j^2+\kappa j$ (`coupled_step_bound`). Integrating over the first step: $\mathbb E d_1^2\le(1+4\kappa+2\kappa^2)(x-x^c)^2$ (the same bound with $j=0$), and $j\sim\mathrm{Po}(h\lambda(x^c))$ has $\mathbb E j\le\ell$, $\mathbb E j^2\le\ell+\ell^2$.

MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledChain_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §8: after $k$ coarse steps the coupled paths satisfy $\mathbb E[(x_{2k}-x^c_{2k})^2]\le B\sum_{i<k}A^i$
MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledChain_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §8, p. 55: "the first step is to express the coarse path Poisson variate as the sum of two Poisson variates, $P(h\lambda(x^c_n))$ corresponding to the first and second fine path timesteps. For the first of the two fine timesteps, the coarse and fine path Poisson variates are coupled by defining two Poisson variates based on the minimum of the two reactions rates, and the absolute difference, $P_1=P\big(h\min(\lambda(x_n),\lambda(x^c_n))\big)$, $P_2=P\big(h|\lambda(x_n)-\lambda(x^c_n)|\big)$, and then using $P_1$ as the Poisson variate for the path with the smaller rate, and $P_1+P_2$ for the path with the larger rate."

Let $\lambda:\mathbb N\to[0,\infty)$ be the propensity function and $h\ge0$ the fine time step. In the coupled simulation (`coupledChain`) both paths start at $x_0$, and each coarse step of size $2h$ is made of two fine steps (`coupledTwoStep`): in each, the fine increment, of rate $h\lambda(x)$ at the current fine state $x$, is coupled (`coupledIncr`) with one half of the coarse increment, of rate $h\lambda(x^c)$ at the coarse state $x^c$ at the start of the coarse step. Expectations of nonnegative quantities are lower integrals. Let $\kappa\ge0$ and $\ell\in\mathbb R$ be such that the scaled rates satisfy $|h\lambda(x)-h\lambda(y)|\le\kappa|x-y|$ and $h\lambda(y)\le\ell$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb N$ (for a $K$-Lipschitz propensity bounded by $\Lambda$: $\kappa=hK$, $\ell=h\Lambda$). Then for every $k$, the coupled paths after $k$ coarse steps from $(x_0,x_0)$ satisfy
$$
\mathbb E\big[(x_{2k}-x^c_{2k})^2\big]\le B\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}A^i,\qquad A=(1+4\kappa+2\kappa^2)^2,\quad B=(\kappa+2\kappa^2)(\ell+\ell^2)+\kappa\ell .
$$
MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledChain_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §8, pp. 55–56 (after D.F. Anderson and D.J. Higham, Multilevel Monte Carlo for continuous time Markov chains, with applications in biochemical kinetics, Multiscale Model. Simul. 10 (2012) 146–179).
MLMC.lintegral_sq_coupledChain_le.explanation: Induction on $k$ along the recursion of `coupledChain` (a bind of `coupledTwoStep`): integrate the bound of `lintegral_sq_coupledTwoStep_le` against the law after $k$ coarse steps, a probability measure (`coupledChain_univ`), and use $A\sum_{i<k}A^i+1=\sum_{i\le k}A^i$ (`geom_sum_succ`). At $k=0$ both paths are at $x_0$.

MLMC.coupledChain_sq_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §8 (Anderson–Higham): for a Lipschitz, bounded propensity the Poisson-coupled fine and coarse tau-leaping paths are $O(h)$ apart in mean square
MLMC.coupledChain_sq_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §8, p. 56: "This elegant approach naturally gives a small difference in the Poisson variates when the difference in rates is small, and leads to a very effective multilevel algorithm with a correction variance which is $O(h)$, leading to an $O(\varepsilon^{-2}(\log\varepsilon)^2)$ complexity."

Let $\lambda:\mathbb N\to[0,\infty)$ be the propensity function and $h\ge0$ the fine time step. In the coupled simulation (`coupledChain`) both paths start at $x_0$, and each coarse step of size $2h$ is made of two fine steps (`coupledTwoStep`): in each, the fine increment, of rate $h\lambda(x)$ at the current fine state $x$, is coupled (`coupledIncr`) with one half of the coarse increment, of rate $h\lambda(x^c)$ at the coarse state $x^c$ at the start of the coarse step. Expectations of nonnegative quantities are lower integrals. Let $\lambda$ be $K$-Lipschitz, $|\lambda(x)-\lambda(y)|\le K|x-y|$, and bounded by $\Lambda$, and let $T\ge0$ be the final time. Then there is $c\ge0$ (depending only on $K$, $\Lambda$, $T$) such that for every time step $0\le h\le1$, every number $k$ of coarse steps with $2kh\le T$, and every $x_0$, the square difference $(x_{2k}-x^c_{2k})^2$ is integrable and
$$
\mathbb E\big[(x_{2k}-x^c_{2k})^2\big]\le c\,h .
$$
MLMC.coupledChain_sq_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §8, pp. 55–56 (after D.F. Anderson and D.J. Higham, Multilevel Monte Carlo for continuous time Markov chains, with applications in biochemical kinetics, Multiscale Model. Simul. 10 (2012) 146–179).
MLMC.coupledChain_sq_le.explanation: Apply `lintegral_sq_coupledChain_le` with $\kappa=hK$ and $\ell=h\Lambda$. As $h\le1$, $B\le h^2B_0$ with $B_0=(K+2K^2)(\Lambda+\Lambda^2)+K\Lambda$; $\sum_{i<k}A^i\le kA^k$; and $A^k=(1+4hK+2h^2K^2)^{2k}\le e^{2k(4hK+2h^2K^2)}\le e^{T(4K+2K^2)}$ since $2kh\le T$. So the bound is at most $h^2B_0\,k\,e^{T(4K+2K^2)}\le h\,B_0Te^{T(4K+2K^2)}$, as $kh\le T$; the lower integral being finite, the square is integrable and its integral is the same number.

MLMC.variance_coupledChain_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §8: with the Poisson coupling, the correction $\Phi(x_T)-\Phi(x^c_T)$ of tau-leaping MLMC has variance $O(h)$ for a Lipschitz payoff
MLMC.variance_coupledChain_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §8, p. 56: "This elegant approach naturally gives a small difference in the Poisson variates when the difference in rates is small, and leads to a very effective multilevel algorithm with a correction variance which is $O(h)$, leading to an $O(\varepsilon^{-2}(\log\varepsilon)^2)$ complexity."

Let $\lambda:\mathbb N\to[0,\infty)$ be the propensity function and $h\ge0$ the fine time step. In the coupled simulation (`coupledChain`) both paths start at $x_0$, and each coarse step of size $2h$ is made of two fine steps (`coupledTwoStep`): in each, the fine increment, of rate $h\lambda(x)$ at the current fine state $x$, is coupled (`coupledIncr`) with one half of the coarse increment, of rate $h\lambda(x^c)$ at the coarse state $x^c$ at the start of the coarse step. Expectations of nonnegative quantities are lower integrals. Let $\lambda$ be $K$-Lipschitz and bounded by $\Lambda$, $T\ge0$, and let the payoff $\Phi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\Phi(x)-\Phi(y)|\le L|x-y|$. Then there is $c\ge0$ such that for every $0\le h\le1$, every $k$ with $2kh\le T$ and every $x_0$,
$$
\mathbb V\big[\Phi(x_{2k})-\Phi(x^c_{2k})\big]\le c\,h .
$$
MLMC.variance_coupledChain_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §8, pp. 55–56 (after D.F. Anderson and D.J. Higham, Multilevel Monte Carlo for continuous time Markov chains, with applications in biochemical kinetics, Multiscale Model. Simul. 10 (2012) 146–179).
MLMC.variance_coupledChain_le.explanation: The law of the coupled paths is a probability measure (`coupledChain_univ`), so $\mathbb V[X]\le\mathbb E[X^2]$; and $(\Phi(x)-\Phi(y))^2\le L^2(x-y)^2$. Apply `coupledChain_sq_le` and take $L^2c$.

MLMC.tauLeaping_level_variance.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §8: $\beta=1$ for tau-leaping MLMC — on level $\ell+1$ the variance of the coupled correction is at most $c\,2^{-\ell}$
MLMC.tauLeaping_level_variance.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §8, p. 56: "This elegant approach naturally gives a small difference in the Poisson variates when the difference in rates is small, and leads to a very effective multilevel algorithm with a correction variance which is $O(h)$, leading to an $O(\varepsilon^{-2}(\log\varepsilon)^2)$ complexity."

Let $T\ge0$ be the final time. On level $\ell+1$ the coupled simulation uses the fine step $h_{\ell+1}=T2^{-(\ell+1)}$ over $2^\ell$ coarse steps, so that the coarse path is the level-$\ell$ chain (`tauLeaping_level`). Let the propensity $\lambda$ be $K$-Lipschitz and bounded by $\Lambda$, and the payoff $\Phi$ be $L$-Lipschitz. Then there is $c\ge0$ such that for every level with $h_{\ell+1}\le1$ and every $x_0$,
$$
\mathbb V\big[\Phi(x_T)-\Phi(x^c_T)\big]\le c\,2^{-\ell} .
$$
With the rates $\alpha=\gamma=1$ this is the case $\beta=\gamma$ of Theorem 1, the complexity $O(\varepsilon^{-2}(\log\varepsilon)^2)$ (`tauLeaping_complexity`).
MLMC.tauLeaping_level_variance.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §8, pp. 55–56 (after D.F. Anderson and D.J. Higham, Multilevel Monte Carlo for continuous time Markov chains, with applications in biochemical kinetics, Multiscale Model. Simul. 10 (2012) 146–179).

MLMC.tendsto_method1MSE.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §3.4: with uniform intervals the mean-square error of method 1 tends to $0$ as $d\to\infty$, for $f$ monotone on $(0,1)$ as $\Phi^{-1}$ is
MLMC.tendsto_method1MSE.natural_language_statement:
Haas–Giles (2025), §3.4, p. 7: "As illustrated by Figure 1 and the convergence analysis from [12], as $d$ tends to infinity, the uniform intervals give MSE$\to0$ and the dyadic intervals give MSE$\to C$, for some positive constant $C$. The latter is because with our simple dyadic segmentation, when $d$ increases by 1 the MSE is reduced only in the interval closest to 0, so the error due to the other intervals remains the same."

Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ (standing for $\Phi^{-1}$) be such that $f$ and $f^2$ are integrable on $[0,1]$. For $d\in\mathbb N$ let $u_j=2^{-d}j$ and $\mathcal I_j=[u_j,u_{j+1}]$ ($j<2^d$) be the uniform intervals, and $Z_j=2^d\int_{u_j}^{u_{j+1}}f(u)\,du$ the LUT values (15) of method 1. If $f$ is monotone (non-decreasing) on $(0,1)$, then
$$
\sum_{j<2^d}\int_{u_j}^{u_{j+1}}\big(Z_j-f(u)\big)^2du\ \longrightarrow\ 0\qquad(d\to\infty).
$$
MLMC.tendsto_method1MSE.source: I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §3.3–§3.4, pp. 6–8, (15), (18)–(19).
MLMC.tendsto_method1MSE.explanation: On an interval inside $(0,1)$ both $f$ and its mean $Z_j$ lie between the values of $f$ at the ends, so the error there is at most $2^{-d}(f(u_{j+1})-f(u_j))^2$; summing and telescoping, the interior intervals contribute at most $2^{-d}(f(1-2^{-d})-f(2^{-d}))^2$ (`method1MSE_le`). Each end interval contributes at most $\int f^2$ over it, which tends to $0$ by continuity of the primitive of $f^2$. By monotonicity, $2^{-d}f(2^{-d})^2\le\int_0^{2^{-d}}f^2+2^{-d}f(1/2)^2$ and similarly at $1$ (`mul_sq_le_left`, `mul_sq_le_right`).

MLMC.dyadic_mse_ge.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §3.4: on a dyadic interval where $f$ is strongly concave, the method-3 error with values $a+bj$ is at least a constant $c>0$ for all $d$, $a$, $b$
MLMC.dyadic_mse_ge.natural_language_statement:
Haas–Giles (2025), §3.4, p. 7: "As illustrated by Figure 1 and the convergence analysis from [12], as $d$ tends to infinity, the uniform intervals give MSE$\to0$ and the dyadic intervals give MSE$\to C$, for some positive constant $C$. The latter is because with our simple dyadic segmentation, when $d$ increases by 1 the MSE is reduced only in the interval closest to 0, so the error due to the other intervals remains the same."

Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ (standing for $\Phi^{-1}$) be such that $f$ and $f^2$ are integrable on $[0,1]$. For $d\in\mathbb N$ let $u_j=2^{-d}j$ and $\mathcal I_j=[u_j,u_{j+1}]$ ($j<2^d$) be the uniform intervals, and $Z_j=2^d\int_{u_j}^{u_{j+1}}f(u)\,du$ the LUT values (15) of method 1. Let $k\in\mathbb N$ and $\mu>0$ be such that $f$ is strongly concave on the dyadic interval $[2^{-(k+1)},2^{-k}]$ in the form
$$
\mu s^2\le 2f(u+s)-f(u)-f(u+2s)\qquad\text{whenever }2^{-(k+1)}\le u,\ s\ge0,\ u+2s\le2^{-k}.
$$
(For $\Phi^{-1}$ this holds on $[2^{-(k+1)},2^{-k}]$ for $k\ge2$, where $(\Phi^{-1})''=\Phi^{-1}/\varphi(\Phi^{-1})^2\le2\pi\,\Phi^{-1}(1/4)<0$.) For $d\ge k+3$ the intervals $\mathcal I_j$ inside the dyadic interval are those with $2^{d-k-1}\le j<2^{d-k}$; method 3 takes the values $a+bj$ on them. Then there is $c>0$ such that for every $d\ge k+3$ and all $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
$$
\sum_{2^{d-k-1}\le j<2^{d-k}}\int_{u_j}^{u_{j+1}}\big(a+bj-f(u)\big)^2du\ \ge\ c ,
$$
namely $c=\mu^2\,2^{-5(k+3)}/6$.
MLMC.dyadic_mse_ge.source: I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §3.3–§3.4, pp. 6–8, (15), (18)–(19).
MLMC.dyadic_mse_ge.explanation: By (18) the error on $\mathcal I_j$ is at least $2^{-d}r_j^2$ with $r_j=a+bj-Z_j$. With the spacing $m=2^{d-k-3}$ and $s=u_m=2^{-(k+3)}$, an affine sequence has zero second differences, so $r_j-2r_{j+m}+r_{j+2m}=2Z_{j+m}-Z_j-Z_{j+2m}$, and by the concavity, averaged over $\mathcal I_j$, this is at least $\mu s^2$ (`lutValue_second_diff_ge`). Then $(\mu s^2)^2\le6(r_j^2+r_{j+m}^2+r_{j+2m}^2)$; summing over the first quarter of the dyadic interval gives $m(\mu s^2)^2\le6\sum_jr_j^2$, and $2^{-d}m=s$.

MLMC.method3_mse_ge.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §3.4: the mean-square error of method 3 (affine values on a dyadic interval where $f$ is strongly concave) is at least a constant $c>0$ for every $d\ge k+3$
MLMC.method3_mse_ge.natural_language_statement:
Haas–Giles (2025), §3.4, p. 8: "Also with dyadic intervals, the MSE value cannot be arbitrarily small, which might limit the number of levels where this method is relevant."

Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ (standing for $\Phi^{-1}$) be such that $f$ and $f^2$ are integrable on $[0,1]$. For $d\in\mathbb N$ let $u_j=2^{-d}j$ and $\mathcal I_j=[u_j,u_{j+1}]$ ($j<2^d$) be the uniform intervals, and $Z_j=2^d\int_{u_j}^{u_{j+1}}f(u)\,du$ the LUT values (15) of method 1. Let $k\in\mathbb N$ and $\mu>0$ be such that $f$ is strongly concave on the dyadic interval $[2^{-(k+1)},2^{-k}]$ in the form
$$
\mu s^2\le 2f(u+s)-f(u)-f(u+2s)\qquad\text{whenever }2^{-(k+1)}\le u,\ s\ge0,\ u+2s\le2^{-k}.
$$
(For $\Phi^{-1}$ this holds on $[2^{-(k+1)},2^{-k}]$ for $k\ge2$, where $(\Phi^{-1})''=\Phi^{-1}/\varphi(\Phi^{-1})^2\le2\pi\,\Phi^{-1}(1/4)<0$.) For $d\ge k+3$ the intervals $\mathcal I_j$ inside the dyadic interval are those with $2^{d-k-1}\le j<2^{d-k}$; method 3 takes the values $a+bj$ on them. Then there is $c>0$ such that for every $d\ge k+3$ and every $w:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ which is affine on the indices of the dyadic interval ($w_j=a+bj$ for $2^{d-k-1}\le j<2^{d-k}$, for some $a,b$),
$$
\sum_{j<2^d}\int_{u_j}^{u_{j+1}}\big(w_j-f(u)\big)^2du\ \ge\ c .
$$
MLMC.method3_mse_ge.source: I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §3.3–§3.4, pp. 6–8, (15), (18)–(19).
MLMC.method3_mse_ge.explanation: The terms of the sum are nonnegative, so it is at least the sum over the intervals of the dyadic interval, where $w_j=a+bj$; apply `dyadic_mse_ge`.

MLMC.method3_mse_not_tendsto_zero.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §3.4: with dyadic intervals the MSE cannot be arbitrarily small — the method-3 mean-square error does not tend to $0$ as $d\to\infty$
MLMC.method3_mse_not_tendsto_zero.natural_language_statement:
Haas–Giles (2025), §3.4, p. 8: "Also with dyadic intervals, the MSE value cannot be arbitrarily small, which might limit the number of levels where this method is relevant."

Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ (standing for $\Phi^{-1}$) be such that $f$ and $f^2$ are integrable on $[0,1]$. For $d\in\mathbb N$ let $u_j=2^{-d}j$ and $\mathcal I_j=[u_j,u_{j+1}]$ ($j<2^d$) be the uniform intervals, and $Z_j=2^d\int_{u_j}^{u_{j+1}}f(u)\,du$ the LUT values (15) of method 1. Let $k\in\mathbb N$ and $\mu>0$ be such that $f$ is strongly concave on the dyadic interval $[2^{-(k+1)},2^{-k}]$ in the form
$$
\mu s^2\le 2f(u+s)-f(u)-f(u+2s)\qquad\text{whenever }2^{-(k+1)}\le u,\ s\ge0,\ u+2s\le2^{-k}.
$$
(For $\Phi^{-1}$ this holds on $[2^{-(k+1)},2^{-k}]$ for $k\ge2$, where $(\Phi^{-1})''=\Phi^{-1}/\varphi(\Phi^{-1})^2\le2\pi\,\Phi^{-1}(1/4)<0$.) For $d\ge k+3$ the intervals $\mathcal I_j$ inside the dyadic interval are those with $2^{d-k-1}\le j<2^{d-k}$; method 3 takes the values $a+bj$ on them. Let $w_d:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$, for each $d$, be affine on the indices $2^{d-k-1}\le j<2^{d-k}$ ($w_d(j)=a_d+b_dj$ there). Then
$$
\sum_{j<2^d}\int_{u_j}^{u_{j+1}}\big(w_d(j)-f(u)\big)^2du\ \not\longrightarrow\ 0\qquad(d\to\infty).
$$
MLMC.method3_mse_not_tendsto_zero.source: I.-B. Haas and M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §3.3–§3.4, pp. 6–8, (15), (18)–(19).
MLMC.method3_mse_not_tendsto_zero.explanation: By `method3_mse_ge` the error is at least $c>0$ for every $d\ge k+3$, so it cannot eventually be below $c$.

MLMC.map_backIter_eq_map_fwdIter.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §10.1: the chain started $n$ steps in the past has the law of the chain after $n$ steps, $Z_n\overset{d}{=}X_n$
MLMC.map_backIter_eq_map_fwdIter.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §10.1, p. 61: "the Markov chain $\{X_n\}$ in a metric space with metric $d$ is defined by $X_0=x$, $X_{n+1}=\phi_n(X_n)$, $n\ge0$ where $\{\phi_n\}$ is a sequence of iid random functions. Furthermore, it is assumed that the $\phi$'s are contracting on average in the sense that $\sup_{x\ne y}\mathbb E\big[(d(\phi_n(x),\phi_n(y))/d(x,y))^{2\gamma}\big]<1$ for some $\gamma\in(0,1)$. Under these conditions, it is known that the distribution of $X_n$ converges weakly to that of a limit random variable $X_\infty$".

Let $(\alpha,d)$ be a complete separable metric space with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra, $E$ a measurable space, $\varphi:\alpha\times E\to\alpha$ jointly measurable, and $\xi_0,\xi_1,\dots$ independent random variables with values in $E$ and common law $\nu$, on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathbb P)$. Let $x_0\in\alpha$, let $X_0=x_0$, $X_{n+1}=\varphi(X_n,\xi_n)$ be the chain, and let $Z_n=\varphi(\cdot,\xi_0)\circ\varphi(\cdot,\xi_1)\circ\cdots\circ\varphi(\cdot,\xi_{n-1})(x_0)$ be the chain started $n$ steps in the past (the level samples of Glynn and Rhee). Then for every $n\in\mathbb N$, $Z_n$ and $X_n$ have the same law.
MLMC.map_backIter_eq_map_fwdIter.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §10.1, p. 61 (after P.W. Glynn and C.-H. Rhee, Exact estimation for Markov chain equilibrium expectations, 2014).
MLMC.map_backIter_eq_map_fwdIter.explanation: $Z_n$ is the forward chain driven by the noises in reverse order, $(\xi_{n-1},\dots,\xi_0)$ (`backIter_eq_fwdIter_rev`). The joint law of the i.i.d. noises is the product measure $\nu^{\mathbb N}$, which is invariant under reindexing by a permutation of $\mathbb N$ (`map_revPerm_infinitePi`).
