MLMC.exists_costFactor_lt_one_nestedCost.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §6.1: a cost factor below 1 on every level does not make the nested cost (32) smaller than the standard cost (8) — counterexample
MLMC.exists_costFactor_lt_one_nestedCost.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.1, p. 12: "The numerical results in Figure 5 show that the cost factor for both uniform and optimised bit-widths is smaller than 1 which means that the nested framework is cheaper than the standard Multilevel Monte Carlo." (And p. 12: "the assumption $\tilde C_\ell\ll C_\ell$ might not be relevant for all levels as the cost of the fixed-point operations becomes comparable to the cost of the path generation on the CPU".)

There exist $V,V^\Delta,C,\tilde C:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ with $V_\ell>0$, $C_\ell>0$, $V^\Delta_\ell\ge0$, $\tilde C_\ell\ge0$ and $\sqrt{\tilde C_\ell/C_\ell}+\sqrt{V^\Delta_\ell/V_\ell}<1$ for every $\ell$, such that for every $L\in\mathbb N$ and every $\varepsilon\ne0$
$$
\varepsilon^{-2}\Big(\sum_{\ell=0}^L\sqrt{V_\ell C_\ell}\Big)^2<\varepsilon^{-2}\Big(\sum_{\ell=0}^L\sqrt{V_\ell\tilde C_\ell}+\sqrt{V^\Delta_\ell(C_\ell+\tilde C_\ell)}\Big)^2,
$$
i.e. the nested cost (32) with $\tilde V_\ell=V_\ell$, $C^\Delta_\ell=C_\ell+\tilde C_\ell$ exceeds the standard MLMC cost (8). For instance $V_\ell=C_\ell=1$, $\tilde C_\ell=9/16$, $V^\Delta_\ell=36/625$: the factor is $3/4+6/25=99/100$, the level cost (33) is $3/4+3/10=21/20$.
MLMC.exists_costFactor_lt_one_nestedCost.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.1, p. 12, eq. (32), (33), (34) and (8), Figure 5; the counterexample is the formalization's.
MLMC.exists_costFactor_lt_one_nestedCost.explanation: Take the constant sequences above. $\sqrt{9/16}=3/4$, $\sqrt{36/625}=6/25$, $\sqrt{1\cdot1}=1$, $\sqrt{(36/625)(1+9/16)}=\sqrt{9/100}=3/10$ (`Real.sqrt_sq`). Both sums are $(L+1)$ times the level value, and $(L+1)^2<(L+1)^2(21/20)^2$; multiply by $\varepsilon^{-2}>0$.

MLMC.integral_sq_mul1_sum1_eq.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §6.3, (39): exact second moments $\mathbb E[mul1_i^2]=\sigma^2h\,\mathbb E[\tilde Z_i^2]$ and $\mathbb E[sum1_i^2]=r^2h^2+\sigma^2h\,\mathbb E[\tilde Z_i^2]$
MLMC.integral_sq_mul1_sum1_eq.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.3, p. 13: "assume that $h\ll\sqrt h$ and $\sigma,r,S_0,Z_i=O(1)$, then we obtain $con2,\ mul1,\ sum1,\ mul2\sim\sqrt h$ (39), $con1\sim h$ (40), $S\sim1$ (41). The takeaway is that the variables $S_i$ are the largest."

Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8) computes the geometric Brownian motion path with the intermediary variables $con1=rh$, $con2=\sqrt h\,\sigma$, $mul1_i=con2\cdot Z_i$, $sum1_i=con1+mul1_i$, $mul2_i=S_i\cdot sum1_i$, $S_{i+1}=S_i+mul2_i$, $S_0=s_0$ (`gbmPath r σ h s₀`), so $S_n=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ with $\mathbb E[Y]=0$ (an increment $\tilde Z_i$), $r,\sigma\in\mathbb R$ and $h\ge0$. Then $mul1=\sqrt h\,\sigma Y$ and $sum1=rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Y$ satisfy
$$
\mathbb E\big[(\sqrt h\,\sigma Y)^2\big]=\sigma^2h\,\mathbb E[Y^2],\qquad\mathbb E\big[(rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Y)^2\big]=r^2h^2+\sigma^2h\,\mathbb E[Y^2].
$$
MLMC.integral_sq_mul1_sum1_eq.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.3, p. 13, eq. (39), with Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8).
MLMC.integral_sq_mul1_sum1_eq.explanation: $(\sqrt h\sigma)^2=\sigma^2h$ for $h\ge0$ (`Real.sq_sqrt`); for $sum1$ expand $(a+bY)^2$ and use $\mathbb E[Y]=0$ (`integral_sq_affine_eq`).

MLMC.integral_sq_mul1_sum1_bounds.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §6.3, (39): "$mul1,sum1\sim\sqrt h$" two-sided, $m\sigma^2h\le\mathbb E[mul1^2]\le\sigma^2h$ and $m\sigma^2h\le\mathbb E[sum1^2]\le(r^2+\sigma^2)h$
MLMC.integral_sq_mul1_sum1_bounds.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.3, p. 13: "assume that $h\ll\sqrt h$ and $\sigma,r,S_0,Z_i=O(1)$, then we obtain $con2,\ mul1,\ sum1,\ mul2\sim\sqrt h$ (39), $con1\sim h$ (40), $S\sim1$ (41). The takeaway is that the variables $S_i$ are the largest."

Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8) computes the geometric Brownian motion path with the intermediary variables $con1=rh$, $con2=\sqrt h\,\sigma$, $mul1_i=con2\cdot Z_i$, $sum1_i=con1+mul1_i$, $mul2_i=S_i\cdot sum1_i$, $S_{i+1}=S_i+mul2_i$, $S_0=s_0$ (`gbmPath r σ h s₀`), so $S_n=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ with $\mathbb E[Y]=0$ and $m\le\mathbb E[Y^2]\le1$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$ ($m=1$ for a standard normal increment), $r,\sigma\in\mathbb R$ and $0\le h\le1$. Then
$$
m\sigma^2h\le\mathbb E\big[(\sqrt h\,\sigma Y)^2\big]\le\sigma^2h,\qquad m\sigma^2h\le\mathbb E\big[(rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Y)^2\big]\le(r^2+\sigma^2)h.
$$
So for $\sigma\ne0$ and $m>0$ the mean squares of $mul1_i$ and $sum1_i$ are of exact order $h$, i.e. their root mean squares of order $\sqrt h$.
MLMC.integral_sq_mul1_sum1_bounds.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.3, p. 13, eq. (39), with Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8).
MLMC.integral_sq_mul1_sum1_bounds.explanation: The exact values of `integral_sq_mul1_sum1_eq` give the lower bounds ($\sigma^2h\,m\le\sigma^2h\,\mathbb E[Y^2]$, and $r^2h^2\ge0$); the upper bounds are `integral_sq_mul1_le` and `integral_sq_sum1_le`.

MLMC.integral_gbmPath_eq.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §6.3, (41): the path of Algorithm 1 with independent centred increments has mean $\mathbb E[S_n]=S_0(1+rh)^n$
MLMC.integral_gbmPath_eq.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.3, p. 13: "assume that $h\ll\sqrt h$ and $\sigma,r,S_0,Z_i=O(1)$, then we obtain $con2,\ mul1,\ sum1,\ mul2\sim\sqrt h$ (39), $con1\sim h$ (40), $S\sim1$ (41). The takeaway is that the variables $S_i$ are the largest."

Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8) computes the geometric Brownian motion path with the intermediary variables $con1=rh$, $con2=\sqrt h\,\sigma$, $mul1_i=con2\cdot Z_i$, $sum1_i=con1+mul1_i$, $mul2_i=S_i\cdot sum1_i$, $S_{i+1}=S_i+mul2_i$, $S_0=s_0$ (`gbmPath r σ h s₀`), so $S_n=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and $Z_0,Z_1,\dots$ independent measurable real random variables (the increments $\tilde Z_i$) with $Z_i$ integrable and $\mathbb E[Z_i]=0$. Then for all $r,\sigma,h,s_0\in\mathbb R$ and $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$
\mathbb E[S_n]=s_0(1+rh)^n.
$$
MLMC.integral_gbmPath_eq.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.3, p. 13, eq. (41), with Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8).
MLMC.integral_gbmPath_eq.explanation: $S_n=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\sigma Z_i)$ (`gbmPath_eq_prod`); the factors are independent, so the mean of the product is the product of the means (`integral_prod_of_iIndepFun`), each equal to $1+rh$.

MLMC.integral_sq_gbmPath_mul2_eq_pow.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §6.3, (39)–(41): exact second moments of $S_i$ and $mul2_i$ for the path of Algorithm 1 with i.i.d.-moment increments
MLMC.integral_sq_gbmPath_mul2_eq_pow.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.3, p. 13: "assume that $h\ll\sqrt h$ and $\sigma,r,S_0,Z_i=O(1)$, then we obtain $con2,\ mul1,\ sum1,\ mul2\sim\sqrt h$ (39), $con1\sim h$ (40), $S\sim1$ (41). The takeaway is that the variables $S_i$ are the largest."

Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8) computes the geometric Brownian motion path with the intermediary variables $con1=rh$, $con2=\sqrt h\,\sigma$, $mul1_i=con2\cdot Z_i$, $sum1_i=con1+mul1_i$, $mul2_i=S_i\cdot sum1_i$, $S_{i+1}=S_i+mul2_i$, $S_0=s_0$ (`gbmPath r σ h s₀`), so $S_n=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and $Z_0,Z_1,\dots$ independent measurable real random variables (the increments $\tilde Z_i$) with $Z_i\in L^2$, $\mathbb E[Z_i]=0$ and $\mathbb E[Z_i^2]=v$ for all $i$ ($v=1$ for standard normal increments). Let $r,\sigma,s_0\in\mathbb R$, $h\ge0$ and $i\in\mathbb N$. Then
$$
\mathbb E[S_i^2]=s_0^2\big((1+rh)^2+\sigma^2hv\big)^i,\qquad\mathbb E\big[mul2_i^2\big]=\mathbb E\big[(S_i(rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i))^2\big]=s_0^2\big((1+rh)^2+\sigma^2hv\big)^i\,(r^2h^2+\sigma^2hv).
$$
MLMC.integral_sq_gbmPath_mul2_eq_pow.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.3, p. 13, eq. (39) and (41), with Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8).
MLMC.integral_sq_gbmPath_mul2_eq_pow.explanation: `integral_sq_gbmPath_eq` and `integral_sq_mul2_eq_prod` write the second moments as products of independent factors; each factor is $\mathbb E[(1+rh+\sqrt h\sigma Z_j)^2]=(1+rh)^2+\sigma^2hv$ (`integral_sq_factor_eq`) and $\mathbb E[sum1_i^2]=r^2h^2+\sigma^2hv$ (`integral_sq_mul1_sum1_eq`).

MLMC.gbmPath_size_bounds.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §6.3, (41): "$S\sim1$" two-sided, $|S_0|e^{-2|r|T}\le|\mathbb E S_n|\le|S_0|e^{|r|T}$ and $S_0^2e^{-4|r|T}\le\mathbb E[S_n^2]\le S_0^2e^{(2|r|+r^2+\sigma^2)T}$
MLMC.gbmPath_size_bounds.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.3, p. 13: "assume that $h\ll\sqrt h$ and $\sigma,r,S_0,Z_i=O(1)$, then we obtain $con2,\ mul1,\ sum1,\ mul2\sim\sqrt h$ (39), $con1\sim h$ (40), $S\sim1$ (41). The takeaway is that the variables $S_i$ are the largest."

Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8) computes the geometric Brownian motion path with the intermediary variables $con1=rh$, $con2=\sqrt h\,\sigma$, $mul1_i=con2\cdot Z_i$, $sum1_i=con1+mul1_i$, $mul2_i=S_i\cdot sum1_i$, $S_{i+1}=S_i+mul2_i$, $S_0=s_0$ (`gbmPath r σ h s₀`), so $S_n=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and $Z_0,Z_1,\dots$ independent measurable real random variables (the increments $\tilde Z_i$) with $Z_i\in L^2$, $\mathbb E[Z_i]=0$ and $\mathbb E[Z_i^2]\le1$. Let $r,\sigma,T,s_0\in\mathbb R$, $0\le h\le1$ with $|r|h\le1/2$, and $n\in\mathbb N$ with $nh\le T$. Then
$$
|s_0|\,e^{-2|r|T}\le\big|\mathbb E[S_n]\big|\le|s_0|\,e^{|r|T},\qquad s_0^2\,e^{-4|r|T}\le\mathbb E[S_n^2]\le s_0^2\,e^{(2|r|+r^2+\sigma^2)T}.
$$
All four bounds are independent of $h$: over a fixed time horizon the size of $S$ is of order $1$ (for $s_0\ne0$).
MLMC.gbmPath_size_bounds.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.3, p. 13, eq. (41), with Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8).
MLMC.gbmPath_size_bounds.explanation: $\mathbb E[S_n]=s_0(1+rh)^n$ (`integral_gbmPath_eq`) with $e^{-2|rh|}\le1+rh\le e^{rh}$ for $|rh|\le1/2$ (`exp_neg_two_mul_abs_le_one_add`, `Real.add_one_le_exp`) and $nh\le T$. $\mathbb E[S_n^2]=s_0^2\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[(1+rh+\sqrt h\sigma Z_i)^2]$ (`integral_sq_gbmPath_eq`) with each factor $\ge(1+rh)^2\ge e^{-4|r|h}$ (`exp_neg_le_prod`); the upper bound is `integral_sq_gbmPath_le`.

MLMC.integral_sq_mul2_bounds.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.3, p. 13: "assume that $h\ll\sqrt h$ and $\sigma,r,S_0,Z_i=O(1)$, then we obtain $con2,\ mul1,\ sum1,\ mul2\sim\sqrt h$ (39), $con1\sim h$ (40), $S\sim1$ (41). The takeaway is that the variables $S_i$ are the largest."

Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8) computes the geometric Brownian motion path with the intermediary variables $con1=rh$, $con2=\sqrt h\,\sigma$, $mul1_i=con2\cdot Z_i$, $sum1_i=con1+mul1_i$, $mul2_i=S_i\cdot sum1_i$, $S_{i+1}=S_i+mul2_i$, $S_0=s_0$ (`gbmPath r σ h s₀`), so $S_n=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and $Z_0,Z_1,\dots$ independent measurable real random variables (the increments $\tilde Z_i$) with $Z_i\in L^2$, $\mathbb E[Z_i]=0$ and $m\le\mathbb E[Z_i^2]\le1$ for some $m\in\mathbb R$. Let $r,\sigma,T,s_0\in\mathbb R$, $0\le h\le1$ with $|r|h\le1/2$, and $i\in\mathbb N$ with $ih\le T$. Then $mul2_i=S_i(rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)$ satisfies
$$
s_0^2\,e^{-4|r|T}\,m\sigma^2h\le\mathbb E\big[mul2_i^2\big]\le s_0^2\,e^{(2|r|+r^2+\sigma^2)T}\,(r^2+\sigma^2)\,h.
$$
So for $s_0\sigma\ne0$ and $m>0$ the mean square of $mul2_i$ is of exact order $h$.
MLMC.integral_sq_mul2_bounds.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.3, p. 13, eq. (39), with Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8).
MLMC.integral_sq_mul2_bounds.explanation: $\mathbb E[mul2_i^2]=s_0^2\prod_{j<i}\mathbb E[(1+rh+\sqrt h\sigma Z_j)^2]\cdot\mathbb E[sum1_i^2]$ by independence (`integral_sq_mul2_eq_prod`); the product is $\ge e^{-4|r|T}$ (`exp_neg_le_prod`) and $\mathbb E[sum1_i^2]\ge m\sigma^2h$ (`integral_sq_mul1_sum1_bounds`). The upper bound is `integral_sq_mul2_le` with $ih\le T$.

MLMC.gbmPath_sq_largest.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §6.3: "the variables $S_i$ are the largest" — for small $h$ the mean squares of $con1,con2,mul1,sum1,mul2$ are below that of $S_n$
MLMC.gbmPath_sq_largest.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.3, p. 13: "assume that $h\ll\sqrt h$ and $\sigma,r,S_0,Z_i=O(1)$, then we obtain $con2,\ mul1,\ sum1,\ mul2\sim\sqrt h$ (39), $con1\sim h$ (40), $S\sim1$ (41). The takeaway is that the variables $S_i$ are the largest."

Algorithm 1 (§4.1, p. 8) computes the geometric Brownian motion path with the intermediary variables $con1=rh$, $con2=\sqrt h\,\sigma$, $mul1_i=con2\cdot Z_i$, $sum1_i=con1+mul1_i$, $mul2_i=S_i\cdot sum1_i$, $S_{i+1}=S_i+mul2_i$, $S_0=s_0$ (`gbmPath r σ h s₀`), so $S_n=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and $Z_0,Z_1,\dots$ independent measurable real random variables (the increments $\tilde Z_i$) with $Z_i\in L^2$, $\mathbb E[Z_i]=0$ and $\mathbb E[Z_i^2]\le1$. Let $r,\sigma,T,s_0\in\mathbb R$, $0\le h\le1$ with $|r|h\le1/2$, $i,n\in\mathbb N$ with $ih\le T$ and $nh\le T$, and assume the time step is small:
$$
(r^2+\sigma^2)\big(1+s_0^2e^{(2|r|+r^2+\sigma^2)T}\big)\,h<s_0^2\,e^{-4|r|T}.
$$
Then
$$
(rh)^2,\ (\sqrt h\,\sigma)^2,\ \mathbb E[(\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)^2],\ \mathbb E[(rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)^2],\ \mathbb E\big[(S_i(rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i))^2\big]\ <\ \mathbb E[S_n^2],
$$
i.e. the mean squares of $con1,con2,mul1_i,sum1_i,mul2_i$ are all smaller than that of $S_n$. The smallness condition holds for all sufficiently small $h>0$ when $s_0\ne0$.
MLMC.gbmPath_sq_largest.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.3, p. 13, eq. (39)–(41) and the sentence after them.
MLMC.gbmPath_sq_largest.explanation: The five quantities are at most $K=(r^2+\sigma^2)(1+s_0^2e^{(2|r|+r^2+\sigma^2)T})h$: $r^2h^2\le r^2h$, $\sigma^2h$, `integral_sq_mul1_le`, `integral_sq_sum1_le` and the upper bound of `integral_sq_mul2_bounds`; and $K<s_0^2e^{-4|r|T}\le\mathbb E[S_n^2]$ by `gbmPath_size_bounds`.

MLMC.variance_linearised_indep_eq.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §4.2, (26): under its own assumptions the independent-errors bound is an equality, $\mathbb V[\sum_i\bar x_i\delta x_i]=V_{indep}$
MLMC.variance_linearised_indep_eq.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §4.2, p. 9: "We assume that the sensitivities $\bar x_i$ and the rounding errors $\delta x_i$ are independent … If we assume that the individual errors $\bar x_i\delta x_i$ are independent and use (22) we get the optimistic upper bound on the path error variance (25): $\mathbb V[P-\tilde P]\le\frac1{12}\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbb E[\bar x_i^2]\,4^{e_i-d_i}\triangleq V_{indep}(d_1,\dots,d_m)$ (26)"; §4.1, p. 8, (22): the rounding errors $\delta x_i$ are "uniform variables over $[-2^{e_i-d_i-1},2^{e_i-d_i-1}]$".

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $s$ a finite index set and, for $i\in s$, $e_i\in\mathbb Z$, $d_i\in\mathbb N$ and random variables $\bar x_i\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ (sensitivities) and $\delta x_i$ (rounding errors) such that each $\delta x_i$ is uniformly distributed on $[-2^{e_i-d_i-1},2^{e_i-d_i-1}]$, $\bar x_i$ is independent of $\delta x_i$, and the products $\bar x_i\delta x_i$ ($i\in s$) are pairwise independent. Then
$$
\mathbb V\Big[\sum_{i\in s}\bar x_i\,\delta x_i\Big]=\frac1{12}\sum_{i\in s}\mathbb E[\bar x_i^2]\,4^{e_i-d_i}=V_{indep}.
$$
So the "optimistic upper bound" (26) (`variance_linearised_indep`) holds with equality under its hypotheses.
MLMC.variance_linearised_indep_eq.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §4.1–4.2, pp. 8–9, eq. (22), (25) and (26).
MLMC.variance_linearised_indep_eq.explanation: The variance of the sum of pairwise independent terms is the sum of the variances (`IndepFun.variance_sum`). A symmetric uniform variable has mean $0$ (`integral_of_isUniform_Icc_neg`), so $\mathbb E[\bar x_i\delta x_i]=\mathbb E[\bar x_i]\mathbb E[\delta x_i]=0$ and $\mathbb V[\bar x_i\delta x_i]=\mathbb E[\bar x_i^2]\,\mathbb E[\delta x_i^2]=\mathbb E[\bar x_i^2]\,4^{e_i-d_i}/12$ (`integral_sq_uniform_roundError`).

MLMC.variance_linearised_indep_ge.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §6.3 with (22), (26): $N$ independent rounding errors of fixed precision give a linearised error of variance at least $Nc\,4^{e-d}/12$
MLMC.variance_linearised_indep_ge.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.3, p. 14: "On the contrary, if the bit-widths in the low precision path generation were fixed, starting at a certain level, the accuracy would decrease. Indeed in the fixed precision case the rounding error at each time step of the Euler-Maruyama scheme is of order $O(h^{-1}2^{e_{S,\ell}-d_{S,\ell}})$ [1, 23] (neglecting the effect of approximate random variables) so for large time steps the net error in $S_N$ is dominated by the time step, however for small time steps the rounding errors due to the finite precision are relatively large."

Haas and Giles (2025), §4.2, p. 9: "We assume that the sensitivities $\bar x_i$ and the rounding errors $\delta x_i$ are independent … If we assume that the individual errors $\bar x_i\delta x_i$ are independent and use (22) we get the optimistic upper bound on the path error variance (25): $\mathbb V[P-\tilde P]\le\frac1{12}\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbb E[\bar x_i^2]\,4^{e_i-d_i}\triangleq V_{indep}(d_1,\dots,d_m)$ (26)"; §4.1, p. 8, (22): the rounding errors $\delta x_i$ are "uniform variables over $[-2^{e_i-d_i-1},2^{e_i-d_i-1}]$".

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $s$ a finite index set with $N=|s|$ elements, $e\in\mathbb Z$, $d\in\mathbb N$ (fixed precision), $c\in\mathbb R$, and for $i\in s$ random variables $\bar x_i\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ with $\mathbb E[\bar x_i^2]\ge c$ and $\delta x_i$ uniformly distributed on $[-2^{e-d-1},2^{e-d-1}]$, with $\bar x_i$ independent of $\delta x_i$ and the products $\bar x_i\delta x_i$ pairwise independent. Then
$$
\frac{N\,c\,4^{e-d}}{12}\le\mathbb V\Big[\sum_{i\in s}\bar x_i\,\delta x_i\Big].
$$
The variance of the linearised rounding error grows linearly in the number of rounded operations, e.g. like $h^{-1}$ for the $N=T/h$ time steps of a path.
MLMC.variance_linearised_indep_ge.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.3, p. 14, with §4.1–4.2, pp. 8–9, eq. (22) and (26).
MLMC.variance_linearised_indep_ge.explanation: By `variance_linearised_indep_eq` the variance is $\frac1{12}\sum_{i\in s}\mathbb E[\bar x_i^2]4^{e-d}\ge\frac1{12}Nc\,4^{e-d}$.

MLMC.perturbed_path_sub_mean_variance.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §6.3 with (22), (26): the rounding error of the path of Algorithm 1 with $S$ rounded every step has mean 0 and variance exactly $V_{indep}$
MLMC.perturbed_path_sub_mean_variance.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.3, p. 14: "On the contrary, if the bit-widths in the low precision path generation were fixed, starting at a certain level, the accuracy would decrease. Indeed in the fixed precision case the rounding error at each time step of the Euler-Maruyama scheme is of order $O(h^{-1}2^{e_{S,\ell}-d_{S,\ell}})$ [1, 23] (neglecting the effect of approximate random variables) so for large time steps the net error in $S_N$ is dominated by the time step, however for small time steps the rounding errors due to the finite precision are relatively large."

Haas and Giles (2025), §4.2, p. 9: "We assume that the sensitivities $\bar x_i$ and the rounding errors $\delta x_i$ are independent … If we assume that the individual errors $\bar x_i\delta x_i$ are independent and use (22) we get the optimistic upper bound on the path error variance (25): $\mathbb V[P-\tilde P]\le\frac1{12}\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbb E[\bar x_i^2]\,4^{e_i-d_i}\triangleq V_{indep}(d_1,\dots,d_m)$ (26)"; §4.1, p. 8, (22): the rounding errors $\delta x_i$ are "uniform variables over $[-2^{e_i-d_i-1},2^{e_i-d_i-1}]$".

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $e\in\mathbb Z$, $d\in\mathbb N$, and $Z_k,\rho_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ ($k\in\mathbb N$) measurable, such that the step inputs $(Z_k,\rho_k)\in\mathbb R^2$ are independent across $k$, each $Z_k$ is square-integrable, and each $\rho_k$ is uniformly distributed on $[-2^{e-d-1},2^{e-d-1}]$ (the model (22) of the rounding errors). Let $r,\sigma,h,s_0\in\mathbb R$ and let $\tilde S$ be the path of Algorithm 1 with $S$ rounded after every step, the rounding error being modelled by $\rho_k$: $\tilde S_0=s_0$, $\tilde S_{k+1}=\tilde S_k(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_k)+\rho_k$. Let $S_n=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)$ be the path in exact arithmetic (`gbmPath`). Then for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$
\mathbb E[\tilde S_n-S_n]=0,\qquad\mathbb V[\tilde S_n-S_n]=\frac1{12}\sum_{k<n}\mathbb E\Big[\Big(\prod_{k<j<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_j)\Big)^2\Big]\,4^{e-d},
$$
which is $V_{indep}$ of (26) for the $n$ roundings of $S$, with the sensitivities $\bar x_k=\partial S_n/\partial S_{k+1}=\prod_{k<j<n}(1+sum1_j)$. The terms $\bar x_k\rho_k$ are not independent as (26) assumes, but the formula is exact.
MLMC.perturbed_path_sub_mean_variance.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.3, p. 14, with §4.1–4.2, pp. 8–9, eq. (20), (22) and (26), and Algorithm 1.
MLMC.perturbed_path_sub_mean_variance.explanation: $D_n=\tilde S_n-S_n$ satisfies $D_0=0$, $D_{k+1}=D_k(1+sum1_k)+\rho_k$ (`gbmPath_succ`). $D_n$ is measurable w.r.t. the σ-algebra of the first $n$ step inputs, hence independent of $(Z_n,\rho_n)$ (`indepFun_of_recursion`, via `indep_iSup_of_disjoint`). Induction (`roundError_step`): $D_n\in L^2$, $\mathbb E[D_n]=0$ and $\mathbb E[D_{n+1}^2]=\mathbb E[D_n^2]\mathbb E[(1+sum1_n)^2]+4^{e-d}/12$ (the cross term is $\mathbb E[D_n]\,\mathbb E[(1+sum1_n)\rho_n]=0$). `perturbed_sub_eq` solves the recursion (`integral_sq_roundError_eq_sum`), and $\mathbb E[(\prod_j(1+sum1_j))^2]=\prod_j\mathbb E[(1+sum1_j)^2]$ (`integral_prod_of_iIndepFun`).

MLMC.integral_sq_perturbed_path_sub_boun.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §6.3: with fixed precision the mean-square rounding error of $S_n$ is between $n\frac{4^{e-d}}{12}e^{-4|r|T}$ and $n\frac{4^{e-d}}{12}e^{(2|r|+r^2+\sigma^2)T}$
MLMC.integral_sq_perturbed_path_sub_boun.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.3, p. 14: "On the contrary, if the bit-widths in the low precision path generation were fixed, starting at a certain level, the accuracy would decrease. Indeed in the fixed precision case the rounding error at each time step of the Euler-Maruyama scheme is of order $O(h^{-1}2^{e_{S,\ell}-d_{S,\ell}})$ [1, 23] (neglecting the effect of approximate random variables) so for large time steps the net error in $S_N$ is dominated by the time step, however for small time steps the rounding errors due to the finite precision are relatively large."

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $e\in\mathbb Z$, $d\in\mathbb N$, and $Z_k,\rho_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ ($k\in\mathbb N$) measurable, such that the step inputs $(Z_k,\rho_k)\in\mathbb R^2$ are independent across $k$, each $Z_k$ is square-integrable, and each $\rho_k$ is uniformly distributed on $[-2^{e-d-1},2^{e-d-1}]$ (the model (22) of the rounding errors). Let $r,\sigma,h,s_0\in\mathbb R$ and let $\tilde S$ be the path of Algorithm 1 with $S$ rounded after every step, the rounding error being modelled by $\rho_k$: $\tilde S_0=s_0$, $\tilde S_{k+1}=\tilde S_k(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_k)+\rho_k$. Let $S_n=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)$ be the path in exact arithmetic (`gbmPath`). Assume moreover $\mathbb E[Z_k]=0$ and $\mathbb E[Z_k^2]\le1$ for all $k$, $0\le h\le1$, $|r|h\le1/2$, and let $T\in\mathbb R$, $n\in\mathbb N$ with $nh\le T$. Then
$$
n\,\frac{4^{e-d}}{12}\,e^{-4|r|T}\le\mathbb E\big[(\tilde S_n-S_n)^2\big]\le n\,\frac{4^{e-d}}{12}\,e^{(2|r|+r^2+\sigma^2)T}.
$$
With $n=T/h$ steps the mean-square rounding error is of exact order $h^{-1}4^{e-d}$, so for a fixed bit-width $d$ it grows without bound as $h\to0$; its root mean square is of order $h^{-1/2}2^{e-d}$ (the paper's $O(h^{-1}2^{e-d})$ is the worst-case bound `integral_abs_roundFixed_path_sub_le`).
MLMC.integral_sq_perturbed_path_sub_boun.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.3, p. 14, with (22) (§4.1, p. 8) and Algorithm 1.
MLMC.integral_sq_perturbed_path_sub_boun.explanation: `integral_sq_roundError_eq_sum` gives $\mathbb E[(\tilde S_n-S_n)^2]=\sum_{k<n}\frac{4^{e-d}}{12}\prod_{k<j<n}\mathbb E[(1+sum1_j)^2]$. Each product has at most $n$ factors; each factor is $\ge(1+rh)^2\ge e^{-4|r|h}$ (`integral_sq_factor_eq`, `exp_neg_le_prod`) and the product is $\le e^{(2|r|+r^2+\sigma^2)nh}$ (`prod_integral_sq_factor_le`); use $nh\le T$.

MLMC.strongError_lt_integral_sq_perturbe.theorem_title: Haas–Giles (2025), §6.3: for small time steps the mean-square rounding error with fixed precision exceeds the mean-square discretisation error $\mathbb E[(S_T-S_n)^2]$
MLMC.strongError_lt_integral_sq_perturbe.natural_language_statement:
Haas and Giles (2025), §6.3, p. 14: "On the contrary, if the bit-widths in the low precision path generation were fixed, starting at a certain level, the accuracy would decrease. Indeed in the fixed precision case the rounding error at each time step of the Euler-Maruyama scheme is of order $O(h^{-1}2^{e_{S,\ell}-d_{S,\ell}})$ [1, 23] (neglecting the effect of approximate random variables) so for large time steps the net error in $S_N$ is dominated by the time step, however for small time steps the rounding errors due to the finite precision are relatively large."

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $e\in\mathbb Z$, $d\in\mathbb N$, and $Z_k,\rho_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ ($k\in\mathbb N$) measurable, such that the step inputs $(Z_k,\rho_k)\in\mathbb R^2$ are independent across $k$, each $Z_k$ is square-integrable, and each $\rho_k$ is uniformly distributed on $[-2^{e-d-1},2^{e-d-1}]$ (the model (22) of the rounding errors). Let $r,\sigma,h,s_0\in\mathbb R$ and let $\tilde S$ be the path of Algorithm 1 with $S$ rounded after every step, the rounding error being modelled by $\rho_k$: $\tilde S_0=s_0$, $\tilde S_{k+1}=\tilde S_k(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_k)+\rho_k$. Let $S_n=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma Z_i)$ be the path in exact arithmetic (`gbmPath`). Assume moreover $\mathbb E[Z_k]=0$ for all $k$, $h>0$, $|r|h\le1/2$, and let $T\in\mathbb R$, $n\in\mathbb N$ with $nh=T$ and
$$
C(T)\,h^2<T\,\frac{4^{e-d}}{12}\,e^{-4|r|T},\qquad C(T)=s_0^2\,e^{(2|r|+\sigma^2)T}(|r|+\sigma^2)\big(5(|r|+\sigma^2)T+4\big)
$$
(`gbmStrongConst r σ T s₀`; the condition holds for all small $h$). Let $z=(z_i)_{i\in\mathbb N}$ have the law $N(0,1)^{\otimes\mathbb N}$ (`stdNormalSeq`) and $S_n(z)=s_0\prod_{i<n}(1+rh+\sqrt h\,\sigma z_i)$. Then
$$
\mathbb E_z\Big[\Big(s_0\,e^{(r-\sigma^2/2)T+\sigma\sqrt h\sum_{i<n}z_i}-S_n(z)\Big)^2\Big]<\mathbb E\big[(\tilde S_n-S_n)^2\big]:
$$
the mean-square discretisation error of the Euler–Maruyama path (exact solution $S_T$ driven by the same normal increments) is smaller than the mean-square rounding error. With $h_\ell=T2^{-\ell}$ and a fixed bit-width, from some level on the rounding error dominates.
MLMC.strongError_lt_integral_sq_perturbe.source: I.-B. Haas, M.B. Giles, A nested MLMC framework for efficient simulations on FPGAs, arXiv:2502.07123 (2025), §6.3, p. 14, with (22) (§4.1, p. 8) and Algorithm 1; the strong error bound is M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015), §5.1 (`gbm_em_strong_error`).
MLMC.strongError_lt_integral_sq_perturbe.explanation: The left side is at most $C(T)h$ by `gbm_em_strong_error` (the Euler–Maruyama path `emPath` of GBM equals `gbmPath`). The right side is at least $n\frac{4^{e-d}}{12}e^{-4|r|T}$ (`integral_sq_roundError_ge`), and $C(T)h<n\frac{4^{e-d}}{12}e^{-4|r|T}$ after multiplying by $h>0$, since $nh=T$.

MLMC.abs_midpoint_sub_avg_le_fderiv.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.3: for a payoff on $\mathbb R^d$ with $K$-Lipschitz gradient, $|f(\frac{a+b}2)-\frac12f(a)-\frac12f(b)|\le\frac K8\|a-b\|^2$
MLMC.abs_midpoint_sub_avg_le_fderiv.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.3, p. 42: "Lengthy analysis proves that the average of the fine and antithetic paths is within $O(h)$ of the coarse path, and hence the multilevel variance is $O(h^2)$ for smooth payoffs"

Let $E$ be a real normed space (for instance $\mathbb R^d$) and $f:E\to\mathbb R$ Fréchet differentiable everywhere with derivative $f'(x)\in E^*$, whose derivative is $K$-Lipschitz: $\|f'(y)-f'(x)\|\le K\|y-x\|$ (operator norm; for $E=\mathbb R^d$ this says that $\nabla f$ is $K$-Lipschitz) for all $x,y\in E$. Then for all $a,b\in E$,
$$
\Big|f\Big(\frac{a+b}2\Big)-\frac12f(a)-\frac12f(b)\Big|\le\frac K8\,\|a-b\|^2,
$$
i.e. $|f(a)+f(b)-2f(\frac{a+b}2)|\le\frac K4\|a-b\|^2$: the first-order terms of the fine and antithetic values cancel.

**Formalization Note** The midpoint is `midpoint ℝ a b`; the derivative is `f' : E → E →L[ℝ] ℝ` with `HasFDerivAt f (f' x) x` for all `x`.
MLMC.abs_midpoint_sub_avg_le_fderiv.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.3 "Multi-dimensional SDEs", pp. 39–42, p. 42.
MLMC.abs_midpoint_sub_avg_le_fderiv.explanation: Restrict $f$ to the line $t\mapsto a+t(b-a)$ (`hasDerivAt_lineRestrict`): the restriction has derivative $t\mapsto f'(a+t(b-a))(b-a)$, which is $K\|b-a\|^2$-Lipschitz; the scalar `abs_midpoint_sub_avg_le` on $[0,1]$ gives the bound, since the midpoint is the point $t=\frac12$.

MLMC.abs_antithetic_le_fderiv.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.3: pointwise bound on the antithetic correction $\frac12(f(a)+f(b))-f(c)$ of a smooth payoff of a $d$-dimensional value
MLMC.abs_antithetic_le_fderiv.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.3, p. 42: "Lengthy analysis proves that the average of the fine and antithetic paths is within $O(h)$ of the coarse path, and hence the multilevel variance is $O(h^2)$ for smooth payoffs"

Let $E$ be a real normed space (for instance $\mathbb R^d$) and $f:E\to\mathbb R$ Fréchet differentiable everywhere with derivative $f'(x)\in E^*$, whose derivative is $K$-Lipschitz: $\|f'(y)-f'(x)\|\le K\|y-x\|$ (operator norm; for $E=\mathbb R^d$ this says that $\nabla f$ is $K$-Lipschitz) for all $x,y\in E$. Then for all $a,b,c\in E$ (fine, antithetic and coarse values)
$$
\Big|\frac{f(a)+f(b)}2-f(c)\Big|\le\|f'(c)\|\,\Big\|\frac{a+b}2-c\Big\|+\frac K4\big(\|a-c\|^2+\|b-c\|^2\big).
$$
For $E=\mathbb R$ this is the scalar `abs_antithetic_le`.
MLMC.abs_antithetic_le_fderiv.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.3 "Multi-dimensional SDEs", pp. 39–42, p. 42.
MLMC.abs_antithetic_le_fderiv.explanation: The first-order Taylor bound in a normed space `abs_taylor_fderiv_le`, $|f(y)-f(x)-f'(x)(y-x)|\le\frac K2\|y-x\|^2$ (from `hasDerivAt_lineRestrict` and the scalar `abs_taylor_first_le`), at $c$ for $y=a$ and $y=b$; the two linear terms add up to $2f'(c)(\frac{a+b}2-c)$, bounded by the operator norm.

MLMC.abs_antithetic_le_midpoint.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.3: $|\frac12(f(a)+f(b))-f(c)|\le L\|\frac{a+b}2-c\|+\frac K8\|a-b\|^2$ for a payoff on $\mathbb R^d$ with $\|\nabla f\|\le L$ and $K$-Lipschitz gradient
MLMC.abs_antithetic_le_midpoint.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.3, p. 42: "Lengthy analysis proves that the average of the fine and antithetic paths is within $O(h)$ of the coarse path, and hence the multilevel variance is $O(h^2)$ for smooth payoffs"

Let $E$ be a real normed space (for instance $\mathbb R^d$) and $f:E\to\mathbb R$ Fréchet differentiable everywhere with derivative $f'(x)\in E^*$, whose derivative is $K$-Lipschitz: $\|f'(y)-f'(x)\|\le K\|y-x\|$ (operator norm; for $E=\mathbb R^d$ this says that $\nabla f$ is $K$-Lipschitz) for all $x,y\in E$. Assume moreover $\|f'(x)\|\le L$ for all $x$. Then for all $a,b,c\in E$
$$
\Big|\frac{f(a)+f(b)}2-f(c)\Big|\le L\,\Big\|\frac{a+b}2-c\Big\|+\frac K8\,\|a-b\|^2:
$$
the antithetic correction is controlled by the distance of the average of the fine and antithetic values from the coarse value and by the square of the fine–antithetic difference.
MLMC.abs_antithetic_le_midpoint.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.3 "Multi-dimensional SDEs", pp. 39–42, p. 42.
MLMC.abs_antithetic_le_midpoint.explanation: Write $\frac{f(a)+f(b)}2-f(c)=-(f(m)-\frac12f(a)-\frac12f(b))+(f(m)-f(c))$ with $m=\frac{a+b}2$; bound the first term by `abs_midpoint_sub_avg_le_fderiv` and the second by the mean value inequality (`Convex.norm_image_sub_le_of_norm_hasFDerivWithin_le`).

MLMC.variance_antithetic_le_fderiv.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.3: for a multi-dimensional SDE, if the fine/antithetic average is within $O(h)$ of the coarse value, the antithetic multilevel variance is $O(h^2)$ for smooth payoffs
MLMC.variance_antithetic_le_fderiv.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.3, pp. 39–42: "With multi-dimensional SDEs which do not satisfy the commutativity condition, the Milstein discretisation requires the simulation of Lévy areas … Nevertheless, Giles and Szpruch (2014) have developed an antithetic treatment which achieves a very low variance despite the $O(h^{1/2})$ strong convergence. The estimator which is used is $Y_\ell=N_\ell^{-1}\sum_i\frac12(P_\ell(\omega_i)+P_\ell(\omega^a_i))-P_{\ell-1}(\omega_i)$ … Lengthy analysis proves that the average of the fine and antithetic paths is within $O(h)$ of the coarse path, and hence the multilevel variance is $O(h^2)$ for smooth payoffs, and $O(h^{3/2})$ for the standard European call option."

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $E$ a real normed space with a measurable structure in which open sets are measurable (e.g. $\mathbb R^d$ with its Borel sets), and $A,B,C:\Omega\to E$ measurable (the fine, antithetic and coarse terminal values). Let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ Fréchet differentiable everywhere with derivative $f'(x)\in E^*$, whose derivative is $K$-Lipschitz: $\|f'(y)-f'(x)\|\le K\|y-x\|$ (operator norm; for $E=\mathbb R^d$ this says that $\nabla f$ is $K$-Lipschitz) for all $x,y\in E$. Assume $\|f'(x)\|\le L$ for all $x$, that $\|\frac{A+B}2-C\|^2$, $\|A-C\|^4$, $\|B-C\|^4$ are integrable, and, for some $D_1,D_2,h\in\mathbb R$,
$$
\mathbb E\Big[\Big\|\frac{A+B}2-C\Big\|^2\Big]\le D_1h^2,\qquad\mathbb E\|A-C\|^4\le D_2h^2,\qquad\mathbb E\|B-C\|^4\le D_2h^2.
$$
Then
$$
\mathbb V\Big[\frac{f(A)+f(B)}2-f(C)\Big]\le\Big(2L^2D_1+\frac{K^2D_2}2\Big)h^2,
$$
the constant of the scalar case `variance_antithetic_le`. The path rates (the SDE analysis of Giles and Szpruch) are hypotheses.
MLMC.variance_antithetic_le_fderiv.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.3 "Multi-dimensional SDEs", pp. 39–42, pp. 39 and 42.
MLMC.variance_antithetic_le_fderiv.explanation: Square `abs_antithetic_le_fderiv` with $\|f'(C)\|\le L$ using `sq_le_of_abs_le_add`: $Y^2\le2L^2\|\frac{A+B}2-C\|^2+\frac{K^2}4(\|A-C\|^4+\|B-C\|^4)$; then $\mathbb V[Y]\le\mathbb E[Y^2]$ (`variance_le_expectation_sq`) and integrate.

MLMC.variance_antithetic_le_midpoint.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.3: the antithetic multilevel variance is $O(h^2)$ for smooth payoffs if $\mathbb E\|\frac{A+B}2-C\|^2=O(h^2)$ and $\mathbb E\|A-B\|^4=O(h^2)$
MLMC.variance_antithetic_le_midpoint.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.3, pp. 39–42: "With multi-dimensional SDEs which do not satisfy the commutativity condition, the Milstein discretisation requires the simulation of Lévy areas … Nevertheless, Giles and Szpruch (2014) have developed an antithetic treatment which achieves a very low variance despite the $O(h^{1/2})$ strong convergence. The estimator which is used is $Y_\ell=N_\ell^{-1}\sum_i\frac12(P_\ell(\omega_i)+P_\ell(\omega^a_i))-P_{\ell-1}(\omega_i)$ … Lengthy analysis proves that the average of the fine and antithetic paths is within $O(h)$ of the coarse path, and hence the multilevel variance is $O(h^2)$ for smooth payoffs, and $O(h^{3/2})$ for the standard European call option."

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $E$ a real normed space with a measurable structure in which open sets are measurable (e.g. $\mathbb R^d$ with its Borel sets), and $A,B,C:\Omega\to E$ measurable (the fine, antithetic and coarse terminal values). Let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ Fréchet differentiable everywhere with derivative $f'(x)\in E^*$, whose derivative is $K$-Lipschitz: $\|f'(y)-f'(x)\|\le K\|y-x\|$ (operator norm; for $E=\mathbb R^d$ this says that $\nabla f$ is $K$-Lipschitz) for all $x,y\in E$. Assume $\|f'(x)\|\le L$ for all $x$, that $\|\frac{A+B}2-C\|^2$ and $\|A-B\|^4$ are integrable, and, for some $D_1,D_2,h\in\mathbb R$,
$$
\mathbb E\Big[\Big\|\frac{A+B}2-C\Big\|^2\Big]\le D_1h^2\quad\text{(the average within $O(h)$ of the coarse path)},\qquad\mathbb E\|A-B\|^4\le D_2h^2.
$$
Then
$$
\mathbb V\Big[\frac{f(A)+f(B)}2-f(C)\Big]\le\Big(2L^2D_1+\frac{K^2D_2}{32}\Big)h^2.
$$
Since $\|A-B\|^4\le8(\|A-C\|^4+\|B-C\|^4)$, these hypotheses are weaker than those of `variance_antithetic_le_fderiv` (with $16D_2$ for $D_2$ the bound is the same).
MLMC.variance_antithetic_le_midpoint.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.3 "Multi-dimensional SDEs", pp. 39–42, pp. 39 and 42.
MLMC.variance_antithetic_le_midpoint.explanation: Square `abs_antithetic_le_midpoint`: $Y^2\le(L\|\frac{A+B}2-C\|+\frac K8\|A-B\|^2)^2\le2L^2\|\frac{A+B}2-C\|^2+\frac{K^2}{32}\|A-B\|^4$; then $\mathbb V[Y]\le\mathbb E[Y^2]$ (`variance_le_expectation_sq`) and integrate.

MLMC.abs_call_antithetic_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.3: for the call payoff $g(x)=\max(x-K,0)$, $|\frac12(g(a)+g(b))-g(c)|\le|\frac{a+b}2-c|+\frac14|a-b|\mathbf 1\{K\text{ strictly between }a,b\}$
MLMC.abs_call_antithetic_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.3, p. 42: "Lengthy analysis proves that the average of the fine and antithetic paths is within $O(h)$ of the coarse path, and hence the multilevel variance is $O(h^2)$ for smooth payoffs, and $O(h^{3/2})$ for the standard European call option."

Let $K,a,b,c\in\mathbb R$ and $g(x)=\max(x-K,0)$. Then
$$
\Big|\frac{g(a)+g(b)}2-g(c)\Big|\le\Big|\frac{a+b}2-c\Big|+\begin{cases}\frac14|a-b|&\text{if }\min(a,b)<K<\max(a,b),\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
$$
The constant $\frac14$ is attained ($a=K-t$, $b=K+t$, $c=K$).
MLMC.abs_call_antithetic_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.3 "Multi-dimensional SDEs", pp. 39–42, p. 42.
MLMC.abs_call_antithetic_le.explanation: Split at $m=\frac{a+b}2$: $g$ is $1$-Lipschitz (`abs_max_sub_max_le_abs`), so $|g(m)-g(c)|\le|m-c|$; and the convexity defect $\frac12(g(a)+g(b))-g(m)$ lies in $[0,\frac14|a-b|]$ and vanishes unless $K$ is strictly between $a$ and $b$ (`call_midpoint_defect`, a case analysis).

MLMC.variance_call_antithetic_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.3: the antithetic multilevel variance is $O(h^{3/2})$ for the European call if the fine/antithetic average has a bounded conditional density
MLMC.variance_call_antithetic_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.3, p. 42: "Lengthy analysis proves that the average of the fine and antithetic paths is within $O(h)$ of the coarse path, and hence the multilevel variance is $O(h^2)$ for smooth payoffs, and $O(h^{3/2})$ for the standard European call option."

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $A,B,C:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ measurable (the fine, antithetic and coarse terminal values), $K\in\mathbb R$ and $g(x)=\max(x-K,0)$. Assume that the joint law of $(|A-B|,\frac{A+B}2)$ is dominated by $\mathrm{law}(|A-B|)\otimes\rho_0\,\mathrm{Leb}$ for some $\rho_0\ge0$ (given the fine–antithetic difference, the average has a density at most $\rho_0$; e.g. $|A-B|$ independent of $\frac{A+B}2$ whose density is at most $\rho_0$), that $(\frac{A+B}2-C)^2$ and $|A-B|^3$ are integrable, and, for some $D_1,D_2,h\in\mathbb R$,
$$
\mathbb E\Big[\Big(\frac{A+B}2-C\Big)^2\Big]\le D_1h^2,\qquad\mathbb E|A-B|^3\le D_2h^{3/2}.
$$
Then
$$
\mathbb V\Big[\frac{g(A)+g(B)}2-g(C)\Big]\le2D_1h^2+\frac{\rho_0D_2}8\,h^{3/2}.
$$

**Formalization Note** The domination is `μ.map (fun ω => (|A ω - B ω|, (A ω + B ω) / 2)) ≤ (μ.map fun ω => |A ω - B ω|).prod ((ρ₀ : ℝ≥0∞) • volume)`; $h^{3/2}$ is `h ^ (3 / 2 : ℝ)`. Marginal hypotheses (bounded density of the average, moment bounds) do not suffice for the exponent $3/2$, see `variance_call_antithetic_le_holder`.
MLMC.variance_call_antithetic_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.3 "Multi-dimensional SDEs", pp. 39–42, p. 42.
MLMC.variance_call_antithetic_le.explanation: By `abs_call_antithetic_le`, $Y^2\le2(\frac{A+B}2-C)^2+\frac18|A-B|^2\mathbf 1\{|\frac{A+B}2-K|<\frac12|A-B|\}$ (`between_iff_abs_lt`). The domination and Tonelli (`lintegral_prod`) bound the expectation of the second term: given $|A-B|=d$ the window $|\frac{A+B}2-K|<\frac d2$ has measure at most $\rho_0d$, so $\mathbb E[|A-B|^2\mathbf 1\{\cdot\}]\le\rho_0\mathbb E|A-B|^3$ (`integral_sq_ite_le_of_density`). Conclude with $\mathbb V[Y]\le\mathbb E[Y^2]$.

MLMC.variance_call_antithetic_le_holder.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.3: the antithetic call variance is at most $2\mathbb E[(\frac{A+B}2-C)^2]+\frac18(\mathbb E|A-B|^{2p})^{1/p}\,\mathbb P(K\text{ between }A,B)^{1/q}$
MLMC.variance_call_antithetic_le_holder.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.3, p. 42: "Lengthy analysis proves that the average of the fine and antithetic paths is within $O(h)$ of the coarse path, and hence the multilevel variance is $O(h^2)$ for smooth payoffs, and $O(h^{3/2})$ for the standard European call option."

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $A,B,C:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ measurable (the fine, antithetic and coarse terminal values), $K\in\mathbb R$ and $g(x)=\max(x-K,0)$. Let $p,q>1$ with $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$, assume $(\frac{A+B}2-C)^2$ and $|A-B|^{2p}$ integrable, and let $S=\{\min(A,B)<K<\max(A,B)\}$. Then
$$
\mathbb V\Big[\frac{g(A)+g(B)}2-g(C)\Big]\le2\,\mathbb E\Big[\Big(\frac{A+B}2-C\Big)^2\Big]+\frac18\big(\mathbb E|A-B|^{2p}\big)^{1/p}\,\mathbb P(S)^{1/q}.
$$
With $\mathbb E[(\frac{A+B}2-C)^2]=O(h^2)$, $\mathbb E|A-B|^{2p}=O(h^p)$ and $\mathbb P(S)=O(h^{1/2})$ this is $O(h^{3/2-1/(2p)})$. Such marginal information cannot give $O(h^{3/2})$: for $h<e^{-2}$, $\frac{A+B}2=C=K+V$ with $V$ uniform on $(-1,1)$ and $|A-B|=h^{1/2}\log(1/h)$ if $|V|<h^{1/2}$, $h^{1/2}$ otherwise, gives $\mathbb P(S)=h^{1/2}$, $\mathbb E|A-B|^r=O(h^{r/2})$ for all $r$, and variance at least $\frac{h^{3/2}}{16}((\log\frac1h-2)^2-h^{1/2}\log^2\frac1h)$.
MLMC.variance_call_antithetic_le_holder.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.3 "Multi-dimensional SDEs", pp. 39–42, p. 42.
MLMC.variance_call_antithetic_le_holder.explanation: By `abs_call_antithetic_le`, $Y^2\le2(\frac{A+B}2-C)^2+\frac18|A-B|^2\mathbf 1_S$; Hölder's inequality (`integral_mul_le_Lp_mul_Lq_of_nonneg`) with $|A-B|^2\in L^p$ (`integrable_norm_rpow_iff`) and $\mathbf 1_S\in L^q$ gives $\mathbb E[|A-B|^2\mathbf 1_S]\le(\mathbb E|A-B|^{2p})^{1/p}\mathbb P(S)^{1/q}$; conclude with $\mathbb V[Y]\le\mathbb E[Y^2]$.

MLMC.eulerCubic_growth.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.6: for the drift $-S^3$ and $hS^2\ge2$ the explicit Euler iterates grow at least like $(hS^2-1)^n|S|$
MLMC.eulerCubic_growth.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.6, p. 44: "A related problem is addressed by Hutzenthaler, Jentzen and Kloeden (2013), who are concerned with SDEs such as $dS_t=-S_t^3\,dt+dW_t$, which have a super-linear growth in the drift and/or the volatility. This again leads to numerical instability if a uniform timestep is used. Their solution is to introduce a slight modification to the Euler-Maruyama discretisation which limits the size of the drift term on each level of approximation when $S_t$ is large, to avoid this instability."

Let $\phi_h(S)=S-hS^3$ be the explicit Euler step for the drift $-S^3$ (`eulerDriftStep (fun S => -S ^ 3) h`) and $\phi_h^{[n]}$ its $n$-th iterate. If $h,S\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $hS^2\ge2$, then for every $n\in\mathbb N$
$$
\big|\phi_h^{[n]}(S)\big|\ge(hS^2-1)^n\,|S|
$$
(at least $2^n|S|$ when $hS^2\ge3$), whereas the solutions of the ODE $S'=-S^3$ decay monotonically. The stochastic statement (divergence of the moments of the Euler–Maruyama scheme) is not formalised.
MLMC.eulerCubic_growth.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.6 "Stiff and highly nonlinear SDEs", pp. 43–44, p. 44.
MLMC.eulerCubic_growth.explanation: $\phi_h(x)=x(1-hx^2)$ (`eulerDriftStep_cubic`); by induction $hx_n^2\ge hS^2\ge2$, so $|1-hx_n^2|=hx_n^2-1\ge hS^2-1\ge1$ and $|x_{n+1}|\ge(hS^2-1)|x_n|$.

MLMC.eulerCubic_tendsto_atTop.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.6: for every timestep $h$, the explicit Euler iterates for the drift $-S^3$ from $|S|>\sqrt{2/h}$ tend to infinity
MLMC.eulerCubic_tendsto_atTop.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.6, p. 44: "A related problem is addressed by Hutzenthaler, Jentzen and Kloeden (2013), who are concerned with SDEs such as $dS_t=-S_t^3\,dt+dW_t$, which have a super-linear growth in the drift and/or the volatility. This again leads to numerical instability if a uniform timestep is used. Their solution is to introduce a slight modification to the Euler-Maruyama discretisation which limits the size of the drift term on each level of approximation when $S_t$ is large, to avoid this instability."

Let $\phi_h(S)=S-hS^3$ be the explicit Euler step for the drift $-S^3$ (`eulerDriftStep (fun S => -S ^ 3) h`) and $\phi_h^{[n]}$ its $n$-th iterate. If $hS^2>2$, i.e. $|S|>\sqrt{2/h}$, then $|\phi_h^{[n]}(S)|\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$. So no uniform timestep $h>0$ is stable for all starting values, while the ODE $S'=-S^3$ is globally stable.
MLMC.eulerCubic_tendsto_atTop.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.6 "Stiff and highly nonlinear SDEs", pp. 43–44, p. 44.

MLMC.eulerCubic_bounded.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.6: for the drift $-S^3$, $h\ge0$ and $hS^2\le2$ the explicit Euler iterates stay within $|S|$ (the threshold $\sqrt{2/h}$ is sharp)
MLMC.eulerCubic_bounded.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.6, p. 44: "A related problem is addressed by Hutzenthaler, Jentzen and Kloeden (2013), who are concerned with SDEs such as $dS_t=-S_t^3\,dt+dW_t$, which have a super-linear growth in the drift and/or the volatility. This again leads to numerical instability if a uniform timestep is used. Their solution is to introduce a slight modification to the Euler-Maruyama discretisation which limits the size of the drift term on each level of approximation when $S_t$ is large, to avoid this instability."

Let $\phi_h(S)=S-hS^3$ be the explicit Euler step for the drift $-S^3$ (`eulerDriftStep (fun S => -S ^ 3) h`) and $\phi_h^{[n]}$ its $n$-th iterate. If $h\ge0$ and $hS^2\le2$, then $|\phi_h^{[n]}(S)|\le|S|$ for every $n$. With `eulerCubic_tendsto_atTop` the stability threshold of the explicit step is exactly $|S|=\sqrt{2/h}$ (at $hS^2=2$ the orbit is the 2-cycle $S,-S$).
MLMC.eulerCubic_bounded.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.6 "Stiff and highly nonlinear SDEs", pp. 43–44, p. 44.
MLMC.eulerCubic_bounded.explanation: $\phi_h(x)=x(1-hx^2)$ (`eulerDriftStep_cubic`); by induction $|x_n|\le|S|$, so $0\le hx_n^2\le hS^2\le2$ and $|1-hx_n^2|\le1$.

MLMC.abs_tamedDrift_lt.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.6: taming limits the drift term, $|h\,b(S)/(1+h|b(S)|)|<1$
MLMC.abs_tamedDrift_lt.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.6, p. 44: "A related problem is addressed by Hutzenthaler, Jentzen and Kloeden (2013), who are concerned with SDEs such as $dS_t=-S_t^3\,dt+dW_t$, which have a super-linear growth in the drift and/or the volatility. This again leads to numerical instability if a uniform timestep is used. Their solution is to introduce a slight modification to the Euler-Maruyama discretisation which limits the size of the drift term on each level of approximation when $S_t$ is large, to avoid this instability."

For a drift $b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $h\ge0$ let $\psi_h(S)=S+\frac{h\,b(S)}{1+h|b(S)|}$ be the tamed Euler step (`tamedDriftStep b h`) and $\phi_h(S)=S+h\,b(S)$ the explicit one (`eulerDriftStep b h`); Giles (2015) gives no formula, $\psi_h$ is the taming of Hutzenthaler, Jentzen and Kloeden. For every $b$, $h\ge0$ and $S\in\mathbb R$,
$$
\Big|\frac{h\,b(S)}{1+h|b(S)|}\Big|<1.
$$
MLMC.abs_tamedDrift_lt.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.6 "Stiff and highly nonlinear SDEs", pp. 43–44, p. 44.

MLMC.abs_tamedDriftStep_sub_eulerDriftSt.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.6: taming is a slight modification, $|\psi_h(S)-\phi_h(S)|\le h^2b(S)^2$
MLMC.abs_tamedDriftStep_sub_eulerDriftSt.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.6, p. 44: "A related problem is addressed by Hutzenthaler, Jentzen and Kloeden (2013), who are concerned with SDEs such as $dS_t=-S_t^3\,dt+dW_t$, which have a super-linear growth in the drift and/or the volatility. This again leads to numerical instability if a uniform timestep is used. Their solution is to introduce a slight modification to the Euler-Maruyama discretisation which limits the size of the drift term on each level of approximation when $S_t$ is large, to avoid this instability."

For a drift $b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $h\ge0$ let $\psi_h(S)=S+\frac{h\,b(S)}{1+h|b(S)|}$ be the tamed Euler step (`tamedDriftStep b h`) and $\phi_h(S)=S+h\,b(S)$ the explicit one (`eulerDriftStep b h`); Giles (2015) gives no formula, $\psi_h$ is the taming of Hutzenthaler, Jentzen and Kloeden. For every $b$, $h\ge0$ and $S\in\mathbb R$,
$$
\Big|S+\frac{h\,b(S)}{1+h|b(S)|}-(S+h\,b(S))\Big|\le h^2\,b(S)^2,
$$
so the tamed and explicit steps agree to $O(h^2)$ for bounded $S$.
MLMC.abs_tamedDriftStep_sub_eulerDriftSt.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.6 "Stiff and highly nonlinear SDEs", pp. 43–44, p. 44.
MLMC.abs_tamedDriftStep_sub_eulerDriftSt.explanation: The difference is $-\frac{h\,b(S)\cdot h|b(S)|}{1+h|b(S)|}$, whose absolute value is $\frac{h^2b(S)^2}{1+h|b(S)|}\le h^2b(S)^2$.

MLMC.tamedDriftStep_iterate_bounded.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.6: for an inward drift ($S\,b(S)\le0$) the tamed Euler iterates stay within $\max(|S|,1)$ for every timestep
MLMC.tamedDriftStep_iterate_bounded.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.6, p. 44: "A related problem is addressed by Hutzenthaler, Jentzen and Kloeden (2013), who are concerned with SDEs such as $dS_t=-S_t^3\,dt+dW_t$, which have a super-linear growth in the drift and/or the volatility. This again leads to numerical instability if a uniform timestep is used. Their solution is to introduce a slight modification to the Euler-Maruyama discretisation which limits the size of the drift term on each level of approximation when $S_t$ is large, to avoid this instability."

For a drift $b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $h\ge0$ let $\psi_h(S)=S+\frac{h\,b(S)}{1+h|b(S)|}$ be the tamed Euler step (`tamedDriftStep b h`) and $\phi_h(S)=S+h\,b(S)$ the explicit one (`eulerDriftStep b h`); Giles (2015) gives no formula, $\psi_h$ is the taming of Hutzenthaler, Jentzen and Kloeden. If $S\,b(S)\le0$ for all $S$ (as for $b(S)=-S^3$) and $h\ge0$, then for all $S$ and $n$, $|\psi_h^{[n]}(S)|\le\max(|S|,1)$. Deterministic analogue only: the uniform moment bounds of the tamed Euler–Maruyama scheme are not formalised.
MLMC.tamedDriftStep_iterate_bounded.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.6 "Stiff and highly nonlinear SDEs", pp. 43–44, p. 44.
MLMC.tamedDriftStep_iterate_bounded.explanation: One step (`abs_tamedDriftStep_le`): the increment $u$ satisfies $|u|<1$ (`abs_tamedDrift_lt`) and $Su\le0$, so $|S+u|\le\max(|S|,1)$ by cases on the signs; then induction.

MLMC.tamedCubic_bounded.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.6: for $dS_t=-S_t^3dt+dW_t$ the tamed Euler drift iterates stay within $\max(|S|,1)$ for every timestep $h\ge0$
MLMC.tamedCubic_bounded.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.6, p. 44: "A related problem is addressed by Hutzenthaler, Jentzen and Kloeden (2013), who are concerned with SDEs such as $dS_t=-S_t^3\,dt+dW_t$, which have a super-linear growth in the drift and/or the volatility. This again leads to numerical instability if a uniform timestep is used. Their solution is to introduce a slight modification to the Euler-Maruyama discretisation which limits the size of the drift term on each level of approximation when $S_t$ is large, to avoid this instability."

Let $\psi_h(S)=S-\frac{hS^3}{1+h|S^3|}$ be the tamed Euler step for the drift $-S^3$ (`tamedDriftStep (fun S => -S ^ 3) h`). For every $h\ge0$, $S\in\mathbb R$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, $|\psi_h^{[n]}(S)|\le\max(|S|,1)$, whereas the explicit iterates explode as soon as $hS^2>2$ (`eulerCubic_tendsto_atTop`).
MLMC.tamedCubic_bounded.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.6 "Stiff and highly nonlinear SDEs", pp. 43–44, p. 44.

MLMC.abs_smoothCDF_sub_le_of_bounded.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.7: for a smoothing function with $|g|\le B$ (of either sign), $|C_\delta(x)-\mathbb P(P<x)|\le(1+B)\,\mathbb P(|P-x|\le\delta)$
MLMC.abs_smoothCDF_sub_le_of_bounded.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "The CDF of a scalar output $P$ … $C(x)\equiv\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{P<x}]\equiv\mathbb E[H(x-P)]$, where $H(x)$ is the Heaviside step function. To improve the multilevel variance, this is smoothed to give $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $x<-1$, and $g(x)=1$ for $x>1$. The parameter $\delta$ controls the degree of smoothing. As $\delta\to0$, $g(x/\delta)\to H(x)$, and the accuracy improves but the variance of the multilevel estimator increases."

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $P:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ measurable, and $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$ (`smoothCDF`). Let $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $g(y)=0$ for $y<-1$, $g(y)=1$ for $y>1$ and $|g(y)|\le B$ for all $y$ (no sign condition). Then for every $\delta>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$
$$
\big|C_\delta(x)-\mathbb P(P<x)\big|\le(1+B)\,\mathbb P(|P-x|\le\delta).
$$
The constant is $\sup|g-H|$, which can be $1+B$; the existing `abs_smoothCDF_sub_le` assumes $0\le g\le1$ (constant $1$), which the paper does not.
MLMC.abs_smoothCDF_sub_le_of_bounded.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.7 "CDF and density estimation", p. 46.
MLMC.abs_smoothCDF_sub_le_of_bounded.explanation: Pointwise $|g((x-P)/\delta)-\mathbf 1_{P<x}|\le(1+B)\mathbf 1_{|P-x|\le\delta}$ (outside the window $g((x-P)/\delta)$ equals the indicator), then integrate (`integral_indicator_const`, `abs_integral_le_integral_abs`).

MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF_of_bounded.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.7: for a bounded smoothing function of either sign, $C_\delta(x)\to\mathbb P(P<x)$ as $\delta\to0^+$ when $P$ has no atom at $x$
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF_of_bounded.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "The CDF of a scalar output $P$ … $C(x)\equiv\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{P<x}]\equiv\mathbb E[H(x-P)]$, where $H(x)$ is the Heaviside step function. To improve the multilevel variance, this is smoothed to give $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $x<-1$, and $g(x)=1$ for $x>1$. The parameter $\delta$ controls the degree of smoothing. As $\delta\to0$, $g(x/\delta)\to H(x)$, and the accuracy improves but the variance of the multilevel estimator increases."

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $P:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ measurable, and $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$ (`smoothCDF`). Let $g$ be measurable with $g=0$ on $(-\infty,-1)$, $g=1$ on $(1,\infty)$ and $|g|\le B$, and let $\mathbb P(P=x)=0$. Then $C_\delta(x)\to\mathbb P(P<x)$ as $\delta\to0^+$.
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF_of_bounded.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.7 "CDF and density estimation", p. 46.
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF_of_bounded.explanation: `abs_smoothCDF_sub_le_of_bounded` and $\mathbb P(|P-x|\le\delta)\to\mathbb P(P=x)=0$ (`tendsto_measureReal_abs_sub_le`, continuity of measure along the decreasing sets).

MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF_of_continuous.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.7: for every continuous $g$ with $g=0$ on $(-\infty,-1)$ and $g=1$ on $(1,\infty)$, $C_\delta(x)\to\mathbb P(P<x)$ when $P$ has no atom at $x$
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF_of_continuous.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "The CDF of a scalar output $P$ … $C(x)\equiv\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{P<x}]\equiv\mathbb E[H(x-P)]$, where $H(x)$ is the Heaviside step function. To improve the multilevel variance, this is smoothed to give $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $x<-1$, and $g(x)=1$ for $x>1$. The parameter $\delta$ controls the degree of smoothing. As $\delta\to0$, $g(x/\delta)\to H(x)$, and the accuracy improves but the variance of the multilevel estimator increases."

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $P:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ measurable, and $C_\delta(x)=\mathbb E[g((x-P)/\delta)]$ (`smoothCDF`). Let $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with $g(y)=0$ for $y<-1$ and $g(y)=1$ for $y>1$ (exactly the paper's hypotheses; $g$ may take values outside $[0,1]$), and let $\mathbb P(P=x)=0$. Then $\lim_{\delta\to0^+}C_\delta(x)=\mathbb P(P<x)=C(x)$.
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF_of_continuous.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.7 "CDF and density estimation", p. 46.
MLMC.tendsto_smoothCDF_of_continuous.explanation: $g$ is bounded on the compact $[-1,1]$ (`IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn`) and takes the values $0,1$ outside, so `tendsto_smoothCDF_of_bounded` applies.

MLMC.tendsto_density_multidim.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.7: for a $d$-dimensional output $P$ with density $\rho$ continuous at $x$, $\mathbb E[\delta^{-d}g((x-P)/\delta)]\to\rho(x)$
MLMC.tendsto_density_multidim.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "the density $\rho(x)$ of the scalar output $P$ is given by $\rho(x)=\lim_{\delta\to0}\mathbb E[\delta^{-1}g((x-P)/\delta)]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $|x|>1$, and $\int_{-1}^1g(x)\,dx=1$. This has similarities with kernel density estimation (Silverman 1986), and can also be generalised to multi-dimensional outputs."

Let $F$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space of dimension $d$ with an additive Haar measure $\nu$ (e.g. Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$), $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ a probability space and $P:\Omega\to F$ measurable whose law has a density $\rho:F\to[0,\infty)$ with respect to $\nu$, continuous at $x\in F$. Let $g:F\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with $g(y)=0$ for $\|y\|>1$ and $\int_Fg\,d\nu=1$. Then
$$
\lim_{\delta\to0^+}\mathbb E\Big[\delta^{-d}\,g\Big(\frac{x-P}{\delta}\Big)\Big]=\rho(x).
$$
The paper gives no formula for $d>1$; $\delta^{-d}$ is the normalisation that makes the limit the density. For $d=1$ this is `tendsto_density`.

**Formalization Note** $d$ is `Module.finrank ℝ F`; the law condition is `μ.map P = ν.withDensity (fun y => (ρ y : ℝ≥0∞))`.
MLMC.tendsto_density_multidim.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.7 "CDF and density estimation", p. 46.
MLMC.tendsto_density_multidim.explanation: The density is integrable (mass $1$) and $\mathbb E[\delta^{-d}g(\delta^{-1}(x-P))]=\int\delta^{-d}g(\delta^{-1}(x-y))\rho(y)\,d\nu(y)$. Split $g=\frac12((2A+1)\varphi_1-(2A-1)\varphi_2)$ with $A=\int|g|\ge1$ and nonnegative kernels $\varphi_{1,2}=(2|g|\pm g)/(2A\pm1)$ of integral $1$, and apply Mathlib's peak-function lemma `tendsto_integral_comp_smul_smul_of_integrable'` to each (`tendsto_kernel_integral_signed_multidim`), with $c=\delta^{-1}\to\infty$.

MLMC.tendsto_density_euclidean.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.7: for an $\mathbb R^d$-valued output with density $\rho$ continuous at $x$, $\rho(x)=\lim_{\delta\to0}\mathbb E[\delta^{-d}g((x-P)/\delta)]$
MLMC.tendsto_density_euclidean.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.7, p. 46: "the density $\rho(x)$ of the scalar output $P$ is given by $\rho(x)=\lim_{\delta\to0}\mathbb E[\delta^{-1}g((x-P)/\delta)]$, where $g(x)$ is a continuous function with $g(x)=0$ for $|x|>1$, and $\int_{-1}^1g(x)\,dx=1$. This has similarities with kernel density estimation (Silverman 1986), and can also be generalised to multi-dimensional outputs."

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and $P:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ (Euclidean space, Lebesgue measure) measurable whose law has a density $\rho$ continuous at $x$. Let $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with $g(y)=0$ for $\|y\|>1$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^d}g=1$. Then $\mathbb E[\delta^{-d}g((x-P)/\delta)]\to\rho(x)$ as $\delta\to0^+$.

**Formalization Note** $\mathbb R^d$ is `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)` with `volume`.
MLMC.tendsto_density_euclidean.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.7 "CDF and density estimation", p. 46.

MLMC.lipschitz_european_asian_lookback.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.1: the European, Asian and lookback payoffs are Lipschitz for the sup norm on discrete paths
MLMC.lipschitz_european_asian_lookback.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.1, p. 29: "For Lipschitz payoff functions $P$ (such as European, Asian and lookback options in finance) for which $|P(S_1)-P(S_2)|\le K\|S_1-S_2\|$, we have …"; p. 33: "the Asian option is based on the average value of the underlying asset, the lookback is based on its maximum or minimum value".

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and $K\in\mathbb R$, and equip $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ (discrete paths $x=(x_0,\dots,x_n)$) with the sup norm $\|x\|_\infty=\max_i|x_i|$. Then, for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$,
$$
\big|f(x)-f(y)\big|\le\|x-y\|_\infty\quad\text{for}\quad f(x)=\max(x_n-K,0),\ \ \max\Big(\frac1{n+1}\sum_{i=0}^nx_i-K,0\Big),\ \ \max\big(\max_ix_i-K,0\big),
$$
(the European call, the Asian call and the fixed-strike lookback call), and
$$
\big|f(x)-f(y)\big|\le2\|x-y\|_\infty\quad\text{for}\quad f(x)=x_n-\min_ix_i,\ \ \max_ix_i-x_n
$$
(the floating-strike lookback call and put).

**Formalization Note** Paths are `Fin (n + 1) → ℝ` with Mathlib's product (sup) metric, the constants are `LipschitzWith 1` and `LipschitzWith 2`, and $\max_i$, $\min_i$ are `Finset.univ.sup'` and `Finset.univ.inf'`. The discount factor $e^{-rT}$ of the paper only rescales the constants.
MLMC.lipschitz_european_asian_lookback.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.1 "Euler-Maruyama discretisation", p. 29 (Lipschitz payoffs) and p. 33 (Asian and lookback options).
MLMC.lipschitz_european_asian_lookback.explanation: The call: $|\max(a,0)-\max(b,0)|\le|a-b|$ (`abs_max_sub_max_le_abs`). The average: $|\bar x-\bar y|\le\frac1{n+1}\sum_i|x_i-y_i|\le\|x-y\|_\infty$ (`dist_le_pi_dist`). The maximum: $x_i\le y_i+\|x-y\|_\infty\le\max_jy_j+\|x-y\|_\infty$ for all $i$ (`Finset.sup'_le`), and symmetrically; likewise for the minimum. The payoffs are compositions (`LipschitzWith.comp`, constant $1\cdot1$) and differences (`LipschitzWith.sub`, constant $1+1$) of these with the coordinate map $x\mapsto x_n$ (`LipschitzWith.eval`).

MLMC.variance_lipschitz_payoff_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.1: for a $K$-Lipschitz path payoff, $\mathbb V[P-P_\ell]\le\mathbb E[(P-P_\ell)^2]\le K^2\mathbb E[\|S-\hat S_\ell\|^2]$
MLMC.variance_lipschitz_payoff_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.1, p. 29: "For Lipschitz payoff functions $P$ (such as European, Asian and lookback options in finance) for which $|P(S_1)-P(S_2)|\le K\|S_1-S_2\|$, we have $\mathbb V[P-P_\ell]\le\mathbb E[(P-P_\ell)^2]\le K^2\,\mathbb E\big[\|S-\hat S_\ell\|^2\big]$".

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $E$ a seminormed abelian group (a space of paths, e.g. $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ with the sup norm), $g:E\to\mathbb R$ with $|g(u)-g(w)|\le L\|u-w\|$ for all $u,w$ ($L\ge0$), and $S,\hat S:\Omega\to E$ almost everywhere strongly measurable with $\|S-\hat S\|^2$ integrable. Then
$$
\mathbb V\big[g(S)-g(\hat S)\big]\le\mathbb E\big[(g(S)-g(\hat S))^2\big]\le L^2\,\mathbb E\big[\|S-\hat S\|^2\big].
$$

**Formalization Note** $L$ is an `ℝ≥0` and the hypothesis is `LipschitzWith L g`; $\mathbb V$ is Mathlib's `variance`.
MLMC.variance_lipschitz_payoff_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.1 "Euler-Maruyama discretisation", p. 29.
MLMC.variance_lipschitz_payoff_le.explanation: $|g(S)-g(\hat S)|\le L\,\mathrm{dist}(S,\hat S)=L\|S-\hat S\|$ pointwise (`LipschitzWith.dist_le_mul`, `dist_eq_norm`), and `variance_sub_le_of_lipschitz` with $D=\|S-\hat S\|$ gives both inequalities ($\mathbb V[Y]\le\mathbb E[Y^2]$, then integrate $Y^2\le L^2D^2$); $g(S)-g(\hat S)$ is a.e. strongly measurable because $g$ is continuous.

MLMC.digital_mismatch_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.1: if $X$ has density $\le\rho$ near $K$, then $\mathbb P(\mathbf 1_{X>K}\ne\mathbf 1_{Y>K})\le2\rho\delta+\mathbb P(|X-Y|>\delta)$ and $\le3\rho^{2/3}\mathbb E[(X-Y)^2]^{1/3}$
MLMC.digital_mismatch_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.1, p. 33: "However, noting that the strong error is $O(h_\ell^{1/2})$, and there is a bounded density of paths terminating in the neighbourhood of $K$, there is therefore an $O(h_\ell^{1/2})$ fraction of the samples with the coarse and fine paths on either side of the strike, with $P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}=\pm1$. This gives $V_\ell=O(h^{1/2})$ … the digital option analysis is due to Avikainen (Avikainen 2009)".

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)$ be a finite measure space, $X,Y:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $K,\rho\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$
\mu\big(|X-K|\le\delta\big)\le2\rho\delta\qquad\text{for all }\delta>0
$$
(the density of $X$ is at most $\rho$ near the strike $K$) and $(X-Y)^2$ is integrable. Write $A=\{\mathbf 1_{\{X>K\}}\ne\mathbf 1_{\{Y>K\}}\}$ for the event that $X$ and $Y$ lie on either side of the strike, and $m=\mathbb E[(X-Y)^2]$. Then for every $\delta>0$
$$
\mu(A)\le2\rho\delta+\mu\big(|X-Y|>\delta\big),\qquad \mu(A)\le2\rho\delta+\frac m{\delta^2},
$$
and
$$
\mu(A)\le3\rho^{2/3}m^{1/3}.
$$
With a mean-square strong error $m=O(h)$ this is an $O(h^{1/3})$ fraction; the exponent $1/3$ is the best possible from these hypotheses alone ($X$ uniform on $[-1,1]$, $K=0$, $Y=X-2d\,\mathbf 1_{\{0<X<d\}}$ give $\mu(A)=d/2$, $m=2d^3$). The paper's $O(h^{1/2})$ uses that the error is $O(h^{1/2})$ on (almost) every path; $p$-th moment bounds $\mathbb E|X-Y|^p=O(h^{p/2})$ give $O(h^{p/(2(p+1))})$ (`MLMC.digital_mismatch_le_of_moment`) and Gaussian-type tails give $O((h\log(1/h))^{1/2})$ (`MLMC.digital_mismatch_le_of_tail`).

**Formalization Note** $\mu(\cdot)$ is `μ.real` (the measure as a real number); $X$, $Y$ need not be measurable; $\mathbf 1_{\{x>K\}}$ is `(Set.Ioi K).indicator 1 x`; $\rho^{2/3}$, $m^{1/3}$ are real powers of nonnegative numbers ($\rho\ge0$ follows from the hypothesis).
MLMC.digital_mismatch_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.1, p. 33 (digital option, Figure 5.4 and Table 5.2); the analysis is attributed there to M. Avikainen, On irregular functionals of SDEs and the Euler scheme, Finance Stoch. 13 (2009).
MLMC.digital_mismatch_le.explanation: If the payoffs differ, $K$ lies between $X$ and $Y$, so $|X-K|\le|X-Y|$ and $A\subseteq\{|X-K|\le\delta\}\cup\{|X-Y|>\delta\}$ (`digital_ne_subset`); the union bound gives the first inequality (`measureReal_digital_ne_le`), Chebyshev–Markov (`measureReal_lt_abs_sub_le_div_sq`, from `mul_meas_ge_le_integral_of_nonneg`) the second. With $p=\mu(A)$, taking $\delta=p/(3\rho)$ gives $p\le\frac23p+9\rho^2m/p^2$, i.e. $p^3\le27\rho^2m$ (`digital_pow_three_le_of_forall`; for $\rho=0$ let $\delta\to\infty$), and $p=(p^3)^{1/3}\le(27\rho^2m)^{1/3}=3\rho^{2/3}m^{1/3}$ (`digital_le_three_mul_rpow`).

MLMC.variance_digital_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.1: $\mathbb V[\mathbf 1_{X>K}-\mathbf 1_{Y>K}]\le\mathbb P(\mathbf 1_{X>K}\ne\mathbf 1_{Y>K})\le3\rho^{2/3}\mathbb E[(X-Y)^2]^{1/3}$ when $X$ has density $\le\rho$ near $K$
MLMC.variance_digital_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.1, p. 33: "… there is therefore an $O(h_\ell^{1/2})$ fraction of the samples with the coarse and fine paths on either side of the strike, with $P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}=\pm1$. This gives $V_\ell=O(h^{1/2})$".

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $X,Y:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ measurable, $K,\rho\in\mathbb R$ with $\mathbb P(|X-K|\le\delta)\le2\rho\delta$ for all $\delta>0$, and $(X-Y)^2$ integrable. Let $D=\mathbf 1_{\{X>K\}}-\mathbf 1_{\{Y>K\}}\in\{-1,0,1\}$. Then
$$
\mathbb V[D]\le\mathbb E[D^2]=\mathbb P\big(\mathbf 1_{\{X>K\}}\ne\mathbf 1_{\{Y>K\}}\big)\le3\rho^{2/3}\,\mathbb E\big[(X-Y)^2\big]^{1/3}.
$$

**Formalization Note** $\mathbf 1_{\{x>K\}}$ is `(Set.Ioi K).indicator 1 x`; $\mathbb P(\cdot)$ is `μ.real`.
MLMC.variance_digital_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.1, p. 33.
MLMC.variance_digital_le.explanation: $\mathbb V[D]\le\mathbb E[D^2]$ (`variance_le_expectation_sq`); $D^2$ is the indicator of $\{\mathbf 1_{\{X>K\}}\ne\mathbf 1_{\{Y>K\}}\}$ (`sq_digital_sub_eq_indicator`), a measurable set, so $\mathbb E[D^2]$ is its probability (`integral_indicator_one`, `integral_sq_digital_sub`); the last inequality is `digital_mismatch_le`.

MLMC.variance_digital_levelDiff_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.1: the digital correction $\mathbf 1_{Y_1>K}-\mathbf 1_{Y_2>K}$ has variance $\le3\rho^{2/3}(\mathbb E[(X-Y_1)^2]^{1/3}+\mathbb E[(X-Y_2)^2]^{1/3})$
MLMC.variance_digital_levelDiff_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.1, p. 33: "noting that the strong error is $O(h_\ell^{1/2})$, and there is a bounded density of paths terminating in the neighbourhood of $K$, there is therefore an $O(h_\ell^{1/2})$ fraction of the samples with the coarse and fine paths on either side of the strike, with $P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}=\pm1$".

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ (the exact value) with $\mathbb P(|X-K|\le\delta)\le2\rho\delta$ for all $\delta>0$, and $Y_1,Y_2:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ measurable (the fine and coarse approximations) with $(X-Y_1)^2$, $(X-Y_2)^2$ integrable. Then
$$
\mathbb V\big[\mathbf 1_{\{Y_1>K\}}-\mathbf 1_{\{Y_2>K\}}\big]\le3\rho^{2/3}\Big(\mathbb E\big[(X-Y_1)^2\big]^{1/3}+\mathbb E\big[(X-Y_2)^2\big]^{1/3}\Big).
$$
The density hypothesis is on the exact value only, not on the approximations; $X$ need not be measurable.
MLMC.variance_digital_levelDiff_le.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.1, p. 33.
MLMC.variance_digital_levelDiff_le.explanation: $\mathbb V[D]\le\mathbb P(\mathbf 1_{\{Y_1>K\}}\ne\mathbf 1_{\{Y_2>K\}})$ (`variance_digital_le_measureReal`); if the fine and coarse payoffs differ, one of them differs from $\mathbf 1_{\{X>K\}}$ (`digital_ne_subset_union`), so the union bound and `digital_mismatch_le` for $(X,Y_1)$ and $(X,Y_2)$ give the bound.

MLMC.variance_digital_rate.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.1: a mean-square strong error $\mathbb E[(X-Y_\ell)^2]\le c\,h_\ell$ gives the digital-option variance rate $V_\ell=O(h_\ell^{1/3})$
MLMC.variance_digital_rate.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.1, p. 33: "This gives $V_\ell=O(h^{1/2})$"; §5.2, p. 35: "In the case of a digital option, if we use the natural multilevel estimator then $P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}=O(1)$ for an $O(h_\ell)$ fraction of the paths, giving $V_\ell=O(h_\ell)$".

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $X$ and $Y_\ell$ ($\ell\in\mathbb N$) measurable real random variables, $K,\rho\in\mathbb R$ with $\mathbb P(|X-K|\le\delta)\le2\rho\delta$ for all $\delta>0$, $c\ge0$ and $h_\ell\ge0$ such that $(X-Y_\ell)^2$ is integrable and $\mathbb E[(X-Y_\ell)^2]\le c\,h_\ell$ for every $\ell$ (strong order $\tfrac12$). Then for every $\ell$
$$
\mathbb V\big[\mathbf 1_{\{X>K\}}-\mathbf 1_{\{Y_\ell>K\}}\big]\le3\rho^{2/3}c^{1/3}h_\ell^{1/3},\qquad
\mathbb V\big[\mathbf 1_{\{Y_{\ell+1}>K\}}-\mathbf 1_{\{Y_\ell>K\}}\big]\le3\rho^{2/3}c^{1/3}\big(h_{\ell+1}^{1/3}+h_\ell^{1/3}\big).
$$
So $V_\ell=O(h_\ell^{1/3})$ from the mean-square error alone, weaker than the paper's $O(h_\ell^{1/2})$ (see `MLMC.digital_mismatch_le` for why); for first-order strong convergence ($\mathbb E[(X-Y_\ell)^2]\le c\,h_\ell^2$, Milstein) the same bound gives $O(h_\ell^{2/3})$ in place of the paper's $O(h_\ell)$.
MLMC.variance_digital_rate.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.1, p. 33 and §5.2 (Digital options), p. 35.
MLMC.variance_digital_rate.explanation: `variance_digital_le` and `variance_digital_levelDiff_le`, with $\mathbb E[(X-Y_k)^2]^{1/3}\le(c\,h_k)^{1/3}=c^{1/3}h_k^{1/3}$ (`Real.rpow_le_rpow`, `Real.mul_rpow`); $\rho\ge0$ follows from the hypothesis at $\delta=1$.

MLMC.digital_mismatch_le_of_tail.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.1, Table 5.2: Gaussian tails $\mathbb P(|X-Y|>\delta)\le Ae^{-\delta^2/(Bh)}$ give $\mathbb V[\mathbf 1_{X>K}-\mathbf 1_{Y>K}]\le2\rho\sqrt{Bh\log(1/h)}+Ah$
MLMC.digital_mismatch_le_of_tail.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.1, p. 33, Table 5.2: for the digital option with the Euler–Maruyama discretisation the observed variance rate is $O(h^{1/2})$ and the analysis rate is $O(h^{1/2}\log h)$ ("the digital option analysis is due to Avikainen (Avikainen 2009)").

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $X,Y:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ measurable, $K,\rho,A,B,h\in\mathbb R$ with $B>0$, $0<h<1$, $\mathbb P(|X-K|\le\delta)\le2\rho\delta$ and
$$
\mathbb P\big(|X-Y|>\delta\big)\le A\,e^{-\delta^2/(Bh)}\qquad\text{for all }\delta>0 .
$$
Then
$$
\mathbb V\big[\mathbf 1_{\{X>K\}}-\mathbf 1_{\{Y>K\}}\big]\le\mathbb P\big(\mathbf 1_{\{X>K\}}\ne\mathbf 1_{\{Y>K\}}\big)\le2\rho\sqrt{B\,h\log(1/h)}+A\,h ,
$$
i.e. an $O((h\log(1/h))^{1/2})$ variance. The tail bound is a hypothesis (for the Euler–Maruyama scheme it is SDE theory).
MLMC.digital_mismatch_le_of_tail.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.1, p. 33 and Table 5.2.

MLMC.digital_mismatch_le_of_moment.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.1: a $p$-th moment bound gives $\mathbb V[\mathbf 1_{X>K}-\mathbf 1_{Y>K}]\le(2\rho+1)\,\mathbb E[|X-Y|^p]^{1/(p+1)}$ when $X$ has density $\le\rho$ near $K$
MLMC.digital_mismatch_le_of_moment.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.1, p. 33: "noting that the strong error is $O(h_\ell^{1/2})$, and there is a bounded density of paths terminating in the neighbourhood of $K$, there is therefore an $O(h_\ell^{1/2})$ fraction of the samples with the coarse and fine paths on either side of the strike".

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, $X,Y:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ measurable, $K,\rho\in\mathbb R$ with $\mathbb P(|X-K|\le\delta)\le2\rho\delta$ for all $\delta>0$, and $p\in\mathbb N$ with $|X-Y|^p$ integrable. Then
$$
\mathbb V\big[\mathbf 1_{\{X>K\}}-\mathbf 1_{\{Y>K\}}\big]\le\mathbb P\big(\mathbf 1_{\{X>K\}}\ne\mathbf 1_{\{Y>K\}}\big)\le(2\rho+1)\,\mathbb E\big[|X-Y|^p\big]^{1/(p+1)} .
$$
In particular a strong error of order $\tfrac12$ in $L^p$, $\mathbb E|X-Y|^p\le c\,h^{p/2}$, gives $O(h^{p/(2(p+1))})$, and strong order $\tfrac12$ in every $L^p$ gives every rate below $\tfrac12$.
MLMC.digital_mismatch_le_of_moment.source: M.B. Giles, Multilevel Monte Carlo methods, Acta Numerica 24 (2015) 259–328, doi:10.1017/S096249291500001X, §5.1, p. 33.
MLMC.digital_mismatch_le_of_moment.explanation:
`variance_digital_le_measureReal`; `measureReal_digital_ne_le` with Markov's inequality for the $p$-th moment (`measureReal_lt_abs_sub_le_div_pow`) gives $\mathbb P(
e)\le2ho\delta+m/\delta^p$, $m=\mathbb E|X-Y|^p$. If $m>0$ take $\delta=m^{1/(p+1)}$, so that $m/\delta^p=m^{1/(p+1)}$ (`Real.rpow_natCast`, `Real.rpow_mul`, `Real.rpow_add`); if $m=0$, $\mathbb P(
e)\le2ho\delta$ for every $\delta>0$ forces $\mathbb P(
e)=0$.

MLMC.gbm_digital_variance_le.theorem_title: Giles (2015), §5.1: for GBM with Euler–Maruyama, the digital option's level correction has variance $O(h_\ell^{1/3})$, with explicit constants
MLMC.gbm_digital_variance_le.natural_language_statement:
Giles (2015), §5.1, pp. 30 and 33, Figure 5.4: "the payoff is a digital option with payoff $P(S)\equiv10\exp(-rT)\,H(S_T-K)$, where $H(x)$ is the Heaviside step function … This gives $V_\ell=O(h^{1/2})$".

Let $Z_0,Z_1,\dots$ be the coordinates of $(\mathbb R^{\mathbb N},N(0,1)^{\otimes\mathbb N})$ (`stdNormalSeq`). Let $r,\sigma,s_0,T,K\in\mathbb R$ with $s_0\ne0$, $\sigma\ne0$, $T>0$, and $h_\ell=T2^{-\ell}$. Let $\hat S_\ell(Z)$ = `gbmEM`$(r,\sigma,T,s_0,\ell)$ be the Euler–Maruyama approximation of $dS=rS\,dt+\sigma S\,dW$, $S_0=s_0$, at $T$ after $2^\ell$ steps of size $h_\ell$ driven by the increments $\sqrt{h_\ell}Z_i$, and $\mathrm{pairAvg}(Z)_k=(Z_{2k}+Z_{2k+1})/\sqrt2$ the coarse increments. Let $C(T)=s_0^2e^{(2|r|+\sigma^2)T}(|r|+\sigma^2)(5(|r|+\sigma^2)T+4)$ (`gbmStrongConst`) and
$$
\rho=\frac{e^{(\sigma^2-r)T}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,|s_0|\,|\sigma|\sqrt T}
$$
(the maximum of the lognormal density of $S_T$). Then for every $\ell\in\mathbb N$
$$
\mathbb V\Big[\mathbf 1_{\{\hat S_{\ell+1}(Z)>K\}}-\mathbf 1_{\{\hat S_\ell(\mathrm{pairAvg}(Z))>K\}}\Big]\le3\rho^{2/3}\,C(T)^{1/3}\big(h_{\ell+1}^{1/3}+h_\ell^{1/3}\big),
$$
